stories.body:
Beijing stops short of confirming specific agenda items, but many hope world’s three biggest nuclear powers will talk about denuclearisation

The meeting of Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen this week will cover topics of “groundbreaking significance” including “safeguarding world peace”, the Chinese foreign ministry has said.

The confirmation of Thursday’s trilateral talks, the first of their kind, will take place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit and cement Xi’s status as a global powerbroker as he presides over events in the glittering southern tech hub of Shenzhen.

At the White House, Trump told reporters he would be speaking to his Chinese and Russian counterparts about denuclearisation, the war in Iran, economics, trade and “my favourite subject, Ukraine”. US officials had earlier indicated that Trump would not discuss Russia’s war in Ukraine during the trip.

Many, including the UN secretary general, António Guterres, had hoped the trilateral talks would be used to discuss reductions in nuclear arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers.

In a call this week, China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, “agreed on the importance of meaningful leader-level conversations to advance goals such as peace and denuclearisation”, the US state department said.

China was the last of the three powers to confirm the trilateral meeting was happening, and its statement stopped short of confirming specific agenda items.

“[The leaders] will exchange views in-depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance,” said the foreign ministry spokesperson, Mao Ning. “Stronger communication among China, Russia, and the United States, along ​with managing differences and stabilising relations, serves the interests of all three countries.”

The Kremlin said “the signficance and symbolism of this meeting are hard to overestimate”.

The UN secretary general, António Guterres, said that if the three leaders “really commit themselves to a meaningful denuclearisation, it will be a great achievement for the world”.

However, many analysts have warned to temper expectations of a major breakthrough.

Xi will “bask in the glow of China serving as the convener and agenda-setter”, wrote Brookings’ Ryan Hass in one such take. However, “symbolism may prove more enduring than the substance of this meeting”.

The three leaders would be approaching the talks with very different priorities, Xiaoyu Pu from the University of Nevada told the Guardian.

after newsletter promotion

China has rebuffed previous attempts to become embroiled in nuclear arms talks with ​Russia and the US, which ‌have the larger stockpiles. Trump, though, has said he wants to talk about denuclearisation, as well as the US-Israeli war in Iran. China, a top economic partner of Tehran, has sought to mediate in the conflict, and says avoiding a return to hostilities is a “top priority”.

Trump’s remarks that he wanted to discuss Ukraine could stoke fears voiced by the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, that the trilateral talks could turn into a “Yalta 2, 3, 4 with a redistribution of influence”. Zelenskyy was referring to the 1945 pact between the US, UK and Soviet Union that created spheres of influence in Europe after the second world war.

“Ukraine-Russia is losing 25,000 soldiers a month, so we’ll be talking about that,” Trump said. He also deflected criticism of Putin in his remarks, saying the Kremlin leader could be “a lot tougher” in Ukraine and that he was already “backing down”.

US officials had said Trump was not expected to raise the issue, and the German president, Frank-Walter Steinmeier, said Xi showed “irritation” in a recent meeting when the idea of the trilateral talks covering Ukraine came up.

For Xi, “much of the political benefit” will be simply in “the ability to bring Putin and Trump to the table”, Peter Alexander, the Shanghai-based managing director at Z-Ben Advisors, told CNBC.

The Wall Street Journal reported last week that the Trump administration had pushed back against Beijing’s demands that the summit be tightly scripted, with prepared statements and not much room for discussion.

Sari Arho Havrén, from the Royal United Services Institute thinktank, wrote on X : “China dislikes surprises and wants to ensure neither Trump nor Putin steals the limelight from the host. Moreover, Xi doesn’t want to be dragged into a discussion about Ukraine or anything else he is not prepared for.”

stories.title: US now "comfortable" with children dying of measles as death toll hits 10
stories.summary: International authorities will announce US lost its elimination status Tuesday.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
International authorities will announce US lost its elimination status Tuesday.

Health officials in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin announced two more measles deaths late last week, bringing the national tally of confirmed measles deaths this year to 10. The total includes the deaths of at least four infants: two in Pennsylvania , one in New York , and one in Wisconsin .

Wisconsin health officials said the latest measles death—the second for the state—was in a child. Pennsylvania’s health department did not reveal the age or other details of the latest death—the state’s seventh—besides revealing it was of an unvaccinated resident in Montour County. Overall, the seven deaths in Pennsylvania include two in Jefferson County, three in Lancaster County, and one in Mifflin, in addition to the new death in Montour. An eighth death was reported in Franklin County , but state health officials have not confirmed it.

For all the states with deaths so far, health officials have noted that they’re the first deaths in decades. Multiple outbreaks are underway across the country, pushing the national tally of cases to nearly 5,500 across 47 states and jurisdictions, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Pennsylvania’s case count alone is over 1,500, and Wisconsin is reporting nearly 650.

Lost status

With outbreaks that have been smoldering and flaring since last year, the US has reportedly lost its measles elimination status—as medical and public health experts have widely expected it would. A panel of experts for the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a regional branch of the World Health Organization, convened last week to review US measles data and assess its elimination status. The PAHO is set to announce its conclusion and the review’s other findings on Tuesday, November 17. But sources broke the news to The Wall Street Journal on Friday that the panel had found that the US had indeed lost its status.

An elimination status is determined by international health authorities after a country has gone more than 12 months without continuous spread of a virus. The status is lost when epidemiological and laboratory data indicate that a chain of transmission involving a viral strain with an identical genotype and lineage has continued uninterrupted for 12 months or longer.

The US earned its elimination status in 2000 after hard-fought vaccination campaigns over several decades. But US vaccination rates have slipped below protective levels in recent years, fueled by the rise of anti-vaccine rhetoric and vaccine misinformation from fierce anti-vaccine advocates, including current US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. As vaccination rates slipped, measles cases skyrocketed. The current case tally is the highest seen since 1991.

“Comfortable” with child deaths

In reporting the PAHO’s determination, the Journal quoted Noel Brewer, chair of an independent US committee who presented findings about the country’s measles outbreaks to PAHO, on the country’s lamentable status: “Runaway measles outbreaks in the United States, as well as the needless deaths, are all due to low measles vaccination coverage. We’ve gotten comfortable letting children be stopped by a deadly disease and die from it.”

The US Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to requests to comment about the loss of the elimination status or to answer a question about how anti-vaccine rhetoric and misinformation, including that from Kennedy, has contributed.

Medical and public health experts continue to sharply criticize Kennedy’s and the Trump administration’s poor handling of the ongoing severe outbreaks. The CDC has not held press briefings in efforts to halt the vaccine-preventable illness and promote vaccination. Instead, Kennedy reportedly ordered the CDC to remove measles death data , and the CDC director declined to approve an urgent health alert about the life-threatening risks of measles during pregnancy.

stories.title: Trump backs return of ex-Nvidia boss after 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign launched
stories.summary: A number of tech figures want the board of the AI chip giant to give Jensen Huang his job back.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Donald Trump greeting Jensen Huang in September this year

Published 16 November 2026, 11:45 GMT

US President Donald Trump has said he "would certainly not mind" seeing Jensen Huang handed back his job as allies of the former Nvidia chief executive called for him to be reinstated.

Huang resigned as boss of the AI chip giant last week after the emergence of two affairs, one of which was with a woman suspected of spying for China and another allegedly with one of his employees.

It has created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms, which is a key part of the AI industry and its huge expansion.

But now fellow tech bosses, including SpaceX's Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have backed a campaign to get Nvidia's board to "Bring Jensen Back".

The pair were among more than 175,000 signatories of an open letter calling for the board to reinstate Huang while an ongoing internal probe is conducted.

President Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back.

"I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that," he told reporters as he left the White House.

The president's comments come after the "Stand with Jensen" campaign group, which claims to be made up of current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, demanded the return of the former chief executive.

They expressed concerns the ex-Nvidia boss "was removed without meaningful due process".

Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of an affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy.

However, he resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him.

The scandal-hit tech boss is now discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times , external , though the publication reported Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him.

A representative for Jensen Huang declined to comment on the report. The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment.

The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House.

President Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal broke out, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy".

Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.

The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy.

It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

'China plays games with us, so we play games with China'

On Monday, Trump said he did not know whether the women Huang had an affair with was a spy for China.

"They say she's a spy. I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't, I don't know that." he said.

The Trump administration issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres on Monday, which allow Chinese companies to access advanced AI chips to train AI models ahead of Trump's meeting with China President Xi Jingping.

The new rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for US export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to cut down on them being illegally diverted.

Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.

Trump said he did not think Huang had put national security at risk. "You know, China plays games with us. So we play games with China," he said.

The BBC understands that the likelihood of Huang being reinstated is low while Nvidia's internal investigations are ongoing.

The FBI is also investigating the affair between the former Nvidia boss and Alice Huang, according to Trump.

'A handshake with Jensen'

Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation.

"Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," he posted on X. , external

"Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."

Fellow tech boss Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, sidestepped the question of Huang returning to Nvidia at a conference, saying: "I don't think I know enough to answer that question."

But Altman, who himself was reinstated to his job after being fired back in 2023, said Huang was a "hero of mine".

Shareholders in Nvidia also want Huang back at the company's helm.

Hundreds of billions of pounds have been wiped off the firm's stock market value in recent days, but it is still worth some $3.87 trillion. Its share price was down in early Monday trading.

In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker called for management to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang".

Lord Sarfraz, a member of the UK's House of Lords, has also written to Nvidia's new chair, Harvey Jones, urging the firm's directors to give "serious consideration" to Huang's return following the investigation.

For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday.

Closing post

Time to recap

US President Donald Trump has said he “wouldn’t mind” seeing Jensen Huang reinstated as chief executive of Nvidia .

Speaking just days after Huang resigned after admitting cheating on his wife – and facing claims of an affair with a Chinese spy – Trump said Nvidia’s CEO had learned a lesson.

Trump told reporters:

double quotation mark “I think he learned a big lesson. I guess maybe one lesson is more important than ⁠another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that. “He could return. There’s a big group of ‌people that would like him to return,”

That group includes a collection of tech bosses including Elon Musk , Tim Sweeney , the founder and CEO of the video game publisher Epic Games, and Garry Tan , the president of business incubator Y Combinator. They all signed a letter calling on Nvidia to reinstate Huang.

Trump also suggested that Alice Huang, the first person reported to have had an affair with Jensen Huag, might not be a Chinese spy, as has been alleged.

He told reporters:

double quotation mark “Usually, what happens with that is that ​any woman ‌coming to the country ​that’s a ​beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy. I don’t know that she was a spy at all.”

Trump also insisted he isn’t planning to replace commerce secretary Howard Lutnick,

In a busy day for AI news, the US also issued a rule that will further restrict China’s access to the best AI chips from companies like Nvidia .

A new rule will force require data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil to obtain a US government license to purchase advanced AI chips from Nvidia and other American manufacturers.

Technology stocks have dropped again on Wall Street, as concern grows that the AI trade may be unravelling.

A senior policymaker at the European Central Bank warned there are growing risks from an “abrupt repricing” in markets and big losses if investor sentiment about artificial intelligence sours.

ECB’s vice president Boris Vujcic said the “rapid expansion of AI is creating new challenges for financial stability” in the 21-nation eurozone.

Nvidia’s shares have turned south again – they’re now down 2% at $159.74.

Other tech stocks are weakening too, pulling the Nasdaq Composite down by 2%.

Trump: Won't replace Lutnick

Donald Trump was also asked by reporters if he would replace commerce secretary Howard Lutnick, and replied: “No”.

Lutnick has come under pressure ever since US treasury secretary Scott Bessent blamed the commerce department for the fact the US had not imposed export restrictions on certain Nvidia chips to China.

But Trump backed Lutnick , telling reporters that the commerce secretary “might have delayed” putting Megaspeed on the US trade blacklist, but then suggested that “he was doing that because if you didn’t delay it . . . you could have a blow-up with China”.

Nvidia’s shares are shaking off their early drop, as investors hear Trump’s supportive words for Jensen Huang.

They’re now down just 0.55% at $161.95.

Trump: Wouldn't mind Huang being reinstated as Nvidia CEO

Newsflash: US President ⁠Donald ⁠Trump has declared that he ⁠would ​not ‌mind ‌seeing Jensen ‌Huang reinstated as the chief executive ‌officer of ​Nvidia.

Trump is speaking to reporters now, ahead of his trip to Manila to attend the ASEAN summit.

The president added that the suggestion that Huang could return to Nvidia is not a bad idea. He says the ex-CEO has learned a lesson, and denies that national security has been put at risk.

UPDATE: Trump said:

double quotation mark “I think having Jensen go back – a lot of people are asking Jensen – they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea.”

That’s quite an intervention, as an open letter circulates calling for the chip giant to reinstate Huang.

Trump also said that he doesn’t know that the woman involved with Huang – Alice Huang – was a Chinese spy.

Update: he said:

double quotation mark “Nobody’s proven that she’s a spy. She may not be a spy.”

[Reminder: the New York Times reported last week that secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington in spring this year, warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy]

Nvidia shares drop by 2.67%

Newsflash: Nvidia’s shares have dropped by 2.67% at the start of trading.

They’ve dropped to $158.51 each. That knocks around $100bn off Nvidia’s market capitalisation, lowering it to $3.82trn.

That’s down from $4.5tn a little over a week ago, before news broke that Jensen Huang had conducted an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

Investors have a lot to digest, from the push to have Jensen Huang reinstalled as Nvidia’s CEO ( see here ) to the new US clampdown on remote access to AI chips ( see here ).

There may also be jitters ahead of Nvidia’s financial results, scheduled for tomorrow afternoon.

Tom Stevenson, investment director at Fidelity International, explains:

double quotation mark “This is the anxious backdrop to a week of potentially market-moving events that include the latest figures from Nvidia, the publication of minutes from the latest Fed meeting, and the widely anticipated IPO of Anthropic, the business behind the Claude AI model. “Nvidia’s results are always closely scrutinised. But never more so than in the week after its founder CEO stepped down. The numbers will be good again, with revenues of $108bn pencilled in, 12% more than in the prior quarter. But the attention will be elsewhere, on the future direction of the company under new leadership.

SFO charges eight people over collapse of London Capital & Finance

Newsflash: The UK’s Serious Fraud Office (SFO) has charged eight individuals in connection with its investigation into the collapse of London Capital & Finance Plc (LCF), one of Britain’s biggest retail investment scandals.

The SFO says that Michael Andrew Thomson (53), Simon Hume-Kendall (73), Elten Barker (53), Paul Careless (51), Robert Sedgwick (78) and John Russell-Murphy (52) have each been charged with conspiracy to defraud. Helen Hume-Kendall (64) has been charged with concealing criminal property.

An eighth defendant has been charged with conspiracy to defraud and acting in contravention of a director disqualification undertaking.

The collapse of LCF, which promised high interest rates on “mini-bonds” between 2013 and 2018, cost about 11,600 investors more than £237m, leaving taxpayers to pay a £120m compensation bill.

US announces new rules to limit remote ccess to advanced AI chips

Newsflash: The US Commerce Department has issued a new rule to limit remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips by certain third countries.

The interim final rule (IFR) is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries, the US government says.

The IFR will require licenses to reexport advanced AI chips to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil.

This move follows reports that Singapore-based Megaspeed , the company where suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang worked, had transferred advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies.

The Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry & Security explains:

double quotation mark Rapid advancement in cloud computing and SI infrastructure have made it increasingly possible to access advanced American computing capabilities remotely, including through data centers located outside countries subject to U.S. export restrictions. This IFR addresses this evolving technological landscape by further aligning protections governing remote access to advanced computing capabilities with existing controls on the physical shipment of sensitive American technology.

Marketwatch’s Mark DeCambre has three questions for anyone considering taking up the CEO’s role at Nvidia:

What am I inheriting? What has the board learned about the export concerns and Nvidia’s financing deals? What’s still unresolved?

How much of the company do I actually get to run? Who‘ll be on the board a year from now, and will they back me if I change a strategy that Jensen put in place?

Who can I count on to stay at Nvidia? If Jensen goes to work for a competitor, which of the people I need at Nvidia might take his call?

Insurance industry workers: how is climate-related risk managed in your company?

Whether you’re a modeller, actuary or underwriter, we’d like to hear how the insurance industry is dealing with climate risk – click here for more :

Tensions are building in the markets ahead of the stockmarket float of AI firm Anthropic.

Anthropic is due to launch its shares onto the stock market on Thursday. And having initially hoped for a $2tn valuation, it may come to market at a lower valuation of $1.5bn, or even less….

Trading platform IG are running an “Anthrophic IPO Market Cap” market where customers can take bets on the company’s valuation when it floats.

So far today, the contract is down 0.7% at around $1.359bn.

Chris Beauchamp, Chief Market Analyst at investing and trading platform IG , says:

double quotation mark “IG’s pre-IPO market continues to see interest from buyers, with the price finding a low around $1.4 trillion following last week’s volatility in tech. This represents a significant drop from the $2 trillion level seen at the end of October, but the less ambitious pricing seems preferable to a pricier offering that then struggles on day one. Sentiment is too fragile right now to weather a bad IPO for such a big name. Nvidia’s troubles do not augur well for the rest of the AI complex, making a strong debut for Anthropic more important than ever.”

stories.title: Five EU countries announce migrant deportation centre in Rwanda
stories.summary: Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands have announced a "return hub" for failed asylum seekers.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 16 November 2026, 11:17 GMT

Five EU countries will open a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda next year as part of a broader push to boost removals.

Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to open a "return hub" ready to accept transfers in 2027, the Dutch and Danish governments announced in statements.

The countries said the scheme would apply to migrants staying illegally in their nations who are subject to deportation, with the Dutch government adding it will provide an alternative if deportees cannot be returned to their country of origin.

Deportees will be able to either integrate into Rwandan society or return to their home country, the nations said.

The scheme will apply to people who have exhausted their legal avenues to stay in the five nations - unlike a scrapped British deal that envisaged sending people to Rwanda to have their claims processed. Legal challenges meant the UK deal never took off, and it was eventually junked by the incoming Labour government in 2024 .

Downing Street has not ruled out the UK joining the scheme, saying they will watch it "with interest".

The five countries say the plan to send migrants abroad is in line with EU and international law, but human rights bodies say it could violate migrant rights.

The deal follows a recent EU reform that allowed for the creation of hubs outside of the bloc.

In a joint press conference in Vienna on Monday, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said the five countries wanted to relieve European asylum systems and stop traffickers arranging deadly trips across the Mediterranean.

In a written statement, the Dutch government said the five countries will "only return single men" as part of the first phase of the deal, adding that the focus for the Netherlands "will be on persons from countries of origin in the same region as Rwanda".

Once in Rwanda, people will be able to integrate into society, which means they will have the right of residence, as well as access to education, healthcare, the labour market and the legal system.

Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said the country is commmited to working with European partners to provide a "safe, legal and dignified solution for migrants".

He added that they would also work on "correcting the global imbalance in economic opportunities", which he called a "key driver of irregular migration".

Ahead of the announcement, diplomatic sources told the AFP news agency the hub is expected to initially run as a pilot, hosting about 100 people, with each of the five nations possibly sending about 20 migrants.

The United Nations' International Organisation for Migration (IOM) could play an ancillary role.

"IOM has a long history of providing assistance to migrants in situations of transit, including in complex contexts," an IOM spokesperson said, adding the agency was in discussions with some EU countries "on plans for the establishment of return hubs or similar mechanisms".

With elections approaching in several EU nations, administrations have been under pressure to show they can control migration.

Concerns around security, struggling economies and disillusionment with governing parties have all had a major role in shaping attitudes towards people leaving their home countries .

Human Rights Watch's senior Africa researcher Clementine de Montjoye said the choice of Rwanda would be a cause of concern as it had a "well-established record of repression of dissent, arbitrary detention, ill-treatment in detention" and support for armed rebels in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo.

"Paying Kigali to host a deportation programme would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad."

The independent EU Agency for Fundamental Rights argued any third country hosting a return hub should "respect fundamental rights", including that people should not be sent to a country where they face serious risk of persecution.

Unaccompanied children should not be sent to a return hub, the agency said.

According to the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, there were almost 110,000 irregular border crossings into the EU in the first 10 months of 2026, which represents a 29% decrease compared to the previous year.

In October, about 18,100 crossings were detected, which is about 6% less than October 2025 but 22% more than in September "largely because of a sharp rise in arrivals on the Western African route to the Canary Islands".

stories.title: Jensen Huang allies build a "war room" to get him back at Nvidia
stories.summary: Huang is weighing a return just days after resigning amid a deepening scandal.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Huang is weighing a return just days after resigning amid a deepening scandal.

Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia’s chief executive, as allies in Silicon Valley pressure the company’s board to reinstate him days after the tech executive resigned over reports he had affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and a subordinate.

Huang has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning, according to multiple people familiar with the matter—even as an independent probe by Nvidia’s board investigates the conduct that led to a spectacular leadership crisis at the $4 trillion chip company this week.

One Huang ally told the FT they were putting together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia chief’s return and would try to garner support from the White House.

“Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” they said. The efforts had Huang’s support, they added.

A public campaign to reinstate Huang has gathered steam over the weekend. Tesla and SpaceX chief Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney were among executives backing a public letter demanding that its board “Bring Jensen Back.”

Huang continues to command fierce loyalty from some employees, several of whom have gone public in calling for his return in the days since he resigned and have signed the open letter.

The effort to reinstate Huang is likely to face pushback from key policymakers in Washington, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday calling for a “dramatic shake-up” in leadership at the company after Huang’s departure.

Huang, who lacked the controlling shareholding of other founder-CEOs and was therefore unable to overule any board decision, also faces a board and a management team now led by interim chief executive Colette Kress that is aiming to steady the company ahead of quarterly results on Tuesday.

Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, has triggered deepening scrutiny of Nvidia’s compliance measures when selling its AI chips to customers in Asia who have potential links to China.

Even allies were unsure how to rehabilitate Huang’s reputation. “Having an affair with a subordinate is a fireable offense,” acknowledged one person involved in efforts to reinstate Huang.

The FT reported on Friday that Arm chief Rene Haas has been approached by Nvidia’s board as a potential successor. Nvidia’s board said no “formal” process had been initiated.

Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker—who are Nvidia shareholders—published an open letter to the board on Friday urging them to leave “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.”

The pair, both large investors in the company, cited “the extraordinary success of Jensen Huang’s leadership over a long period of time and given the massive uncertainty associated with recent events surrounding his departure” as reasons for clemency.

Some firms are directing refunds to corporate leadership instead of reimbursing consumers, ProPublica finds

Several companies that received refunds for paying Donald Trump’s tariffs have put those funds towards corporate bonuses instead of reimbursing consumers, an investigation from ProPublica has found.

After analyzing securities filings and earnings calls, ProPublica identified at least nine companies who are said they are receiving tariff refunds and noted they are directing some of those funds to their leadership.

Stanley Black & Decker, a tool company that makes common household products including vacuums, electric drills and measuring tapes, told its consumers they were forced to raise prices because of Trump’s import fees, ProPublica reported. The company is expected to receive at least $298m in tariff reimbursements and indicated some of it will go to bonuses. Executives at TJMaxx and Marshalls, discount department stores that are set to receive tariff refunds, also said the same.

In financial disclosures, Stanley Black & Decker said the refund it received “was partially offset by directly attributable costs for variable incentive compensation”, according to ProPublica. Stanley Black & Decker, TJMaxx and Marshalls did not immediately respond to request for comment.

The Trump administration has refunded at least $100bn to companies since August, about 60% of roughly $131bn in tariffs, after the supreme court ruled that Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs were illegal. The court ruled that the tariffs were unlawful because they overstepped his executive authority and should have required congressional approval.

Some companies immediately sued the US government for refunds after the ruling, though Trump signaled that he would “remember” which companies requested reimbursements and praised companies for holding off. The Trump administration has not specified which companies are receiving refunds, despite requests for information, according to ProPublica.

Though many companies said publicly that they had to increase prices because of tariffs, it has largely been unclear what companies are doing with their tariff refunds.

In its analysis, ProPublica found that almost all the companies that have publicly said they plan to use their tariff reimbursements to refund customers are those that deal directly with other businesses, rather than directly consumers. Some companies have remained “vague” about their plans for the reimbursements and have not specified whether those funds will go towards price decreases or holding back on future increases, according to the report.

Research has shown that US consumers have shouldered some of the cost of tariffs, with the New York Federal Reserve estimating that 26% of tariff increases pass through to consumer prices. The Yale Budget Lab estimated that tariffs cost households about $900 annually under current laws.

Tariffs are one of several of Trump’s economic policies that have proven unpopular with voters, reflected in the widespread victories Democrats notched in the November midterms. A year after Trump’s tariffs were announced, a survey from the Pew Research Center found that 63% of Americans felt little or no confidence in his handling of tariffs.

Republican candidates across the country were largely punished for Trump’s tariffs and other White House decisions that have led to greater inflation. In the Associated Press’s survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters, two-thirds said that Trump’s decisions had fueled inflation, about half of the number of 2022 midterm voters who said the same thing about former president Joe Biden.

stories.body:
Experts say US president may lean toward global affairs after domestic influence curtailed in midterm elections

Donald Trump is embarking on his first overseas trip since his Republican party’s thumping midterm repudiation by US voters, in what may herald a renewed focus on foreign policy for the remainder of his presidency.

The US president will meet his Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, for their first trilateral summit, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum in the Chinese city of Shenzhen. Before that, he will land in Manila in the Philippines on Tuesday for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit.

At the Asean summit, Trump is expected to sign a trade agreement with Thailand , push deals with other countries and lobby fellow leaders to favour the US over China on artificial intelligence.

He will also take part in the first leaders’ meeting of the Quad partnership – consisting of the US, Japan, India and Australia – since he returned to the White House in January 2025.

White House officials said the president would be accompanied to Apec by Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX entrepreneur who spent almost $500m (£380m) unsuccessfully supporting Republican candidates in this month’s midterms. The reason for Musk’s presence has not been explained.

The China leg of the trip will take place amid the continuing fallout from the Nvidia spying scandal , which prompted the company’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, to resign amid revelations he had had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Trump is under pressure to raise the matter with Xi when they hold a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of Apec.

The US president has said he does not plan to bring up the subject ; administration officials insist he will not do so and that the meeting will be dedicated to implementing a trade agreement between the two superpowers.

Huang persuaded the Trump administration to lift restrictions on the sale of Nvidia’s AI chips to China that had been imposed during Joe Biden’s presidency.

Mao Ning, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson, told reporters on Monday that at the trilateral summit, Xi, Trump and Putin “will exchange views in depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance”.

Some analysts have characterised the meeting as a “big three” gathering echoing the 1945 Yalta meeting of Winston Churchill, Franklin D Roosevelt and Joseph Stalin that in effect carved up postwar Europe, between a communist-ruled east and a democratic, capitalist west.

Such a prospect has alarmed Ukraine , which fears that Putin – who initially suggested the trilateral meeting – will use it to persuade Trump and Xi to agree to a settlement of the war with Russia on Moscow’s terms.

However, Trump has said Ukraine will not be up for debate at the meeting and that its main purpose will be to discuss ending the US’s war with Iran and “denuclearisation” – shorthand for a deal among the three powers to limit nuclear arms.

That is believed to be unpalatable to China , which has been increasing its nuclear arsenal, and has signalled an unwillingness to enter into reduction agreements until it is closer to parity with the US and Russia.

after newsletter promotion

Analysts say the main beneficiary of the three-way meeting is likely to be Putin, whose standing will be boosted by being treated on an equal footing by two other leaders whose countries are, in reality, much more powerful.

Expectations of a substantial agreement are low.

Lyle Goldstein, an international affairs fellow and China specialist at Brown University in the US, said the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting would not have a substantive result. “There will be no ‘Yalta’, as many have feared,” he said.

Jonathan Czin, the Michael Armacost chair in foreign policy studies at the Brookings Institution, said Trump’s lame duck status would deter Xi and Putin from trying to reach long-term arrangements with the US.

“Both men know Trump’s time is expiring even more quickly than his leverage – and that he will be irrelevant in a mere 26 months [when his term expires],” Czin told an online Brookings forum . “Why would either man make a deal with a leader whose time and leverage are waning? They will only do it if they think they can pilfer more from Trump diplomatically than they will be able to gain from the next American president.”

Nevertheless, Goldstein – who took soundings on Chinese expectations for the summit in a visit to Shenzhen last week – predicted Trump would follow the pattern of previous presidents by turning increasingly to global affairs while he faces the prospect of his influence on the domestic front being curtailed after the Democrats’ victories in the House of Representatives and the Senate.

“The president has been badly damaged by the election and will have limited prospects for the next two years,” he said. “That may cause him to be more active in foreign policy since he can act in that domain with fewer constraints. It would not surprise me if Trump is ready to go all-out to make some further splash in foreign policy.”

With the risks of reigniting the war with Iran high and the Russia-Ukraine war still resistant to a diplomatic resolution despite White House efforts, Goldstein suggested Trump could attempt “a dramatic foreign policy flourish in Asia”, such as an agreement with Kim Jong-un, the North Korean dictator with whom he has frequently boasted of having a close relationship. Kim is not expected to attend the Apec gathering, although there have been rumours he may appear.

stories.title: Miliband says he won't resign if government approves Rosebank oil field
stories.summary: Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh is to make a decision on Britain's largest untapped oil field.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 16 November 2026, 13:42 GMT

Ed Miliband said he will "definitely not" resign if the government approves the Rosebank oil field, despite previously calling the scheme "climate vandalism".

The foreign secretary told the BBC he would "obey collective responsibility", which requires ministers to publicly support decisions made by the government even if they disagree with them.

A decision on the future of the oil field off Shetland will be taken by Miatta Fahnbulleh, who succeeded Miliband as energy secretary in July.

Some Labour MPs oppose the project, while the Conservatives argue there is a need to "get Britain drilling". Miliband publicly raised his concerns about Rosebank while Labour was in opposition.

Appearing on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Miliband was reminded that in 2023 he said the project would be a "colossal waste of taxpayer money and climate vandalism" , external .

Asked if it could be assumed he would resign if his successor decided to develop Rosebank, Miliband replied: "No, definitely not because I obey collective responsibility.

"Miatta Fahnbulleh will make the decision on this. As you know, it's what they call a quasi-judicial decision so she looks at all the evidence and then reaches a conclusion."

Miliband said he would not "second guess her decision" on Rosebank.

He added he supported the energy secretary recently giving the green light to the Jackdaw gas field after years of uncertainty and a court case.

Pressed further about his previous remarks on Rosebank, Miliband said: "I'm a member of the government and I will abide by collective responsibility on this."

He went on to say there are "direct and very bad impacts at home" for the cost of living linked to Russia's invasion of Ukraine and the Iran conflict.

Miliband added: "What does that teach us? That we can't get economic and energy security from fossil fuels, we've got to keep on with this transition to wind power, solar power, nuclear power; homegrown clean energy we can control."

Catherine Fookes is among a group of Labour MPs, reported to number at least 75, who have signed a letter opposing Rosebank.

The MP for Monmouthshire told Today: "We need to really look at what we're doing and ensure we don't exacerbate our climate challenges and make climate change worse.

"And that's exactly what drilling in the North Sea would do."

Steve Yemm, Labour MP for Mansfield, offered his support to Rosebank and said it would be a "test of whether, as a country, we can support investment and skilled work in the North Sea whilst meeting our climate obligations".

One Labour MP, who is pro Rosebank, said they were increasingly confident the decision would go their way, but added the "gloves will now come off" after Fookes's intervention.

They said people on both sides of the argument had been attempting to avoid so-called "red on red" clashes but predicted Labour MPs would now start to disagree more forcefully in public about the issue.

The same MP accused Miliband of "running two departments" and said the current group of energy ministers were "all his people" and "all coming from the same place".

They said they were becoming increasingly frustrated with Labour MPs who opposed Rosebank and added "Trump is right, we do need to open the North Sea".

Some people in Parliament believe that a decision on the oil field could be made as soon as the end of this month.

Rosebank is Britain's largest untapped oil field and would also produce some gas. It is about 80 miles (128km) north-west of Shetland.

In 2023, the then Conservative UK government granted a licence for Rosebank and a legal challenge followed.

The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that the government had made the approval unlawfully, leaving the current Labour government to make a new decision on whether to give the go-ahead.

If approved, Rosebank is expected to fill up to 500m barrels of oil over its 25-year lifetime.

But prices are determined by international markets, which means there is no guarantee that increased supply would result in cheaper energy bills in the UK.

Environmental campaigners believe approval of Rosebank would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and would have no meaningful impact on the UK's energy security or bills.

They have also argued that Rosebank would be even more damaging for the environment than Jackdaw, as it would produce far more planet-warming greenhouse gases.

The UK is committed to reaching net zero by 2050 - meaning the UK must cut carbon emissions until it removes as much as it produces - and wants to limit global warming to no more than 1.5C above the pre-industrial period.

On Monday, it was announced that gas has begun flowing from the Jackdaw gas field .

Conservative shadow energy secretary Andrew Bowie said: "One gas field does not make an energy strategy.

"Labour cannot claim to back the North Sea while continuing to block new licences, undermine investor confidence, and hammer the industry with a punishing windfall tax."

Bowie added "it is clear that Labour cannot be trusted to deliver the energy security we need" with some of the party's MPs "seemingly poised to rebel" over the approval of Rosebank.

stories.title: Tech Companies Are Trying to Shift the Entire Concept of Privacy (Again)
stories.summary: Privacy, which companies were once happy to claim was all about personal choice, is now primed to affect everyone around you even more than it already did. Meta and Google’s smart glasses can record anything the owner is looking at or use artificial intelligence to describe it. Apple’s* Audio Intelligence feature turns every Apple Watch into a transcription machine that records or summarizes your day. Amazon’s Bee devices take that a step further and can record and transcribe everything. Dozens of other companies are introducing pendants , rings , and other products designed to record, transcribe, or summarize everything we say and do all day long. Privacy has always been a team sport. The actions you take with communication apps , collaborative software , or your cloud backup solutions , have long impacted everyone else you’re interacting with. But moving those choices deeper into the physical world where strangers, colleagues, family, and friends are all now a part of your privacy choices is drastically changing the game. Tech companies want us to accept a reality where one person’s privacy choices (or lack thereof) means you suddenly need to be an expert in consumer tech who understands the capabilities of many devices on the market, how they work, how and if they signal when they’re recording, and what platforms they do or do not connect to. They believe these ambient surveillance devices that work in the background and are designed to look as normal as possible are the future, while they also expect the owners of these devices to use them responsibly and to notify those around them of their capabilities to act within whatever laws their states may have. This is not reasonable, nor how consent works in any practical sense. Let’s break this down by looking at some of the biggest players currently in the game: Apple and Amazon, who have two different takes on transcribing audio throughout the day, as well as Meta and Google, who both have slapped AI and cameras onto eyeglasses. stories.title: Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI
stories.summary: The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. We visit Rockstar Games for a hands-on encounter with the cultural event of the decade – and can confirm it more than lives up to the hype It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto, the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). Grand Theft Auto is now made by a huge team of nearly 5,000 people around the world but its central nervous system is still in Holyrood, in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat. The setting of the latest Grand Theft Auto game really could not be further from the Scottish capital. Grand Theft Auto VI takes us to Vice City in the state of Leonida, a parody of Miami, Florida. It is a neon-soaked metropolis of sleaze and struggle, hard-partying excess juxtaposed with a barely concealed criminal underworld and unpredictable Florida madness. Continue reading...

stories.title: Killer tunes: how Grand Theft Auto conquered the music world
stories.summary: Featuring hundreds of songs from the hippest real-world artists, the radio stations in Rockstar’s crime sagas are as hotly anticipated as the storylines. Contributors including Flying Lotus, Wavves and Nite Jewel reflect on the soundtracks’ curation and impact • The exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI • Crime pays: how GTA became a cultural colossus • Ten movies (and one TV show) that inspired GTA A droptop sports car speeds along a highway blaring 90s west coast rap from its booming sound system. Gradually, the asphalt gives way to rural backwaters, and so the sounds of Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas’s local radio also change: less gangster rap and more twangin’ country – the grizzled croon of Merle Haggard and yearning warble of Patsy Cline. The Grand Theft Auto games are massive, stretching across many, many square miles of virtual terrain. Their soundtracks, relayed mostly via in-game radio stations, are manifold. And these two aspects, plus the personal experiences each player brings to the game, mean everyone has a different favourite musical memory from the smash-hit crime series. For acclaimed electronic musician Flying Lotus, it is all the hours he spent cavorting around 2004’s San Andreas that remain special. “It felt like the first time a game saw a different side of culture – black culture,” he says over the phone. “It felt like we were being seen. And with the extent of the music, all the cool California hip-hop, it felt like someone actually cared.” Continue reading...

stories.title: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
stories.summary: The Nvidia scandal has raised questions over whether advanced AI chips ended up in China, despite US restrictions.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The Nvidia scandal has sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley as well as the political establishment

Published 15 November 2026

Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says.

Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.

Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.

Megaspeed said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".

It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".

Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director of Megaspeed near the end of 2023, according to Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS but it said she was still "practically in control" of the company.

Alice Huang - who is of no relation to Nvidia's former boss - had been investigated by Singapore authorities in February 2025 as part of the country's probe into Megaspeed and other companies.

Also on Sunday, US Congressman John Moolenaar said that Jensen Huang had agreed to testify before the House Select Committee on China, which he chairs, as well as the Foreign Affairs and the Intelligence committees.

The committees had threatened to issue subpoenas to Jensen Huang if he did not comply with their requests to testify.

Moolenaar told CBS, BBC's US partner, that none were ultimately issued.

Jensen Huang's testimony is expected to take place behind close doors, with the dates still being finalised.

Moolenaar said: "That's going to be a very important meeting to understand to what degree privileged information was accessed, and to what degree this potential alleged Chinese spy influenced Nvidia's philosophy and may have had an influence on some of our policies with respect to AI and export controls."

Separately, a group of tech leaders including Space X's Elon Musk, have been trying to rally support to have Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia's chief executive.

A representative forJensen Huang declined to comment on a report in the Financial Times suggesting that he was discussing a comeback to the firm he co-founded.

The BBC understands that the likelihood of him being reinstated is very low while the company's internal investigations are ongoing.

The move would also face scrutiny from Washington, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calling for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.

For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday, 17 November.

On Friday, Bessent blamed the US Commerce Department, led by fellow cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips.

Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process".

The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals.

Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.

Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang.

Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?

Nvidia has been banned from selling its advanced semiconductors to China.

While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.

Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.

Megaspeed said it "designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes". It said this includes "US export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate".

China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.

stories.title: Chicago Is $55 Billion in Debt, With No End in Sight. It’s a Threat to City Services.
stories.summary: The post Chicago Is $55 Billion in Debt, With No End in Sight. It’s a Threat to City Services. appeared first on ProPublica .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.imageAlt: A person sitting in a motorized wheelchair looks at the camera with a serious expression. They are outside on a sunny day, on a sidewalk next to a tree-lined city street. They are wearing sunglasses.
stories.body:
Co-published with WTTW News

Reporting Highlights

Crushing Debt: Chicago’s mismanagement of pensions and heavy reliance on borrowing over decades have created an unrelenting financial burden.

Vicious Cycle: To solve its annual budget crunch, more borrowing is used to fill in holes, including back pay for firefighters and payouts for police misconduct.

Strained Services: Solutions to crises involving public health lack the funding that can improve the lives of Chicagoans, and basic inspections for sidewalks and restaurants fall short.

These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.

When the city of Chicago eventually finishes its spending plan for 2027, $3.9 billion will come right off the top.

Taxpayers will have nothing to show for it. Not a single cent of that money will be used to fill a pothole, pick up a can of garbage, pay a firefighter to respond to an emergency or address lead poisoning in children.

Strapped into a straitjacket made up of the city’s debt, there is nothing Chicago’s mayor or City Council can do about it, forced to spend billions every year simply to stay current on the $55 billion it owes to banks and its pension funds.

No other big city will pay more toward its debt this year or next, according to an analysis by WTTW News and ProPublica. This year, $3.6 billion out of a $16.6 billion budget was consumed by debt.

New York City, with a population three times the size of Chicago’s and a budget more than seven times as big, has $47 billion in debt backed by tax revenues. Los Angeles, which has approximately 1 million more residents than Chicago but a smaller budget, has $1 billion in debt set to be paid back with taxes, records show.

According to all four of the major Wall Street credit-rating agencies, New York’s and Los Angeles’ fiscal health make them much better choices for investors. Chicago’s history of questionable borrowing and budgeting — it chose to either ignore or short its pension payments for years — has undermined its credibility.

Its credit rating now sits just two or three levels above junk status, making the cost of borrowing even more onerous. And the city’s chief financial officer, tasked with managing city debt and relationships with credit agencies, resigned last week in stunning fashion , saying she no longer could continue in the role because it would compromise her “integrity and professional obligations.” She had come from Fitch Ratings, a credit agency, and had been on the job for only three months.

Chicago’s Pension Systems Are Less than 50% Funded

The city is an outlier among other large cities, where most pensions are at least 75% funded.

Options for a financial rescue are limited or unpalatable. Pension obligations, locked in by law and political realities, remain untouchable. There is little public or political appetite to raise property taxes or cut city jobs, particularly among the ranks of police, the city’s largest workforce. A windfall from the city’s still-under-construction casino grows more unlikely than ever.

The office of Mayor Brandon Johnson, who is finishing up his first term in office, blames “reckless financing methods” from past administrations for the city’s financial bind.

“Savings and efficiencies alone cannot solve the city’s persistent structural gap,” the city’s Office of Budget and Management wrote to WTTW and ProPublica in response to questions for this story. In searching for revenue streams, Johnson has sought to impose new taxes on the city’s biggest corporations — an effort that has met stiff resistance.

Tackling the pension crisis, the city since 2023 has paid an additional $1 billion into its four pension funds above what is required by state law, records show, an infusion that the city touts as a stabilizing force.

But, like his predecessors, Johnson continues to rely on borrowing. Since taking office in 2023, Johnson has added $1.9 billion to the city’s debt obligations, according to city data.

That borrowing has “advanced desperately needed investment in economic development and affordable housing in historically underserved communities on the South and West sides,” according to Johnson’s spokesperson.

It also has been used to keep the city functioning. In 2026, for example, Chicago borrowed $166 million to pay firefighters what they were owed for working without a contract — and annual raises — for four years. Officials acknowledged they failed to set enough cash aside annually to cover those widely anticipated costs. The city borrowed an additional $267 million to cover the soaring cost of lawsuits alleging Chicago police officers committed a wide range of misconduct.

In some cases, the Johnson administration has negotiated agreements with its lenders that allow the city to pay only interest for several years, backloading its debt burden.

Chicago’s Debt Payments Were the Largest Category of the City’s Budget in 2026

With so much of the city budget dedicated to debt and pensions — and more cordoned off by federal and state laws that mandate spending for specific purposes, such as transportation — Chicago officials get to decide how to spend just one-third of its annual budget, records show.

The result for residents: Restaurant inspections are lagging. Complaints about crumbling sidewalks and injuries from those hazards pile up, without timely repairs. The city’s Public Health Department doesn’t have enough caseworkers to handle the intensive intervention needed for children suffering from lead poisoning.

The budget pressures are unrelenting. In August, Johnson announced another borrowing plan to fix a budget shortfall that emerged midyear. He blamed the City Council for overestimating the impact of new revenue streams while his council foes accused him of continuing a pattern of questionable borrowing habits.

Amid the finger-pointing, Johnson acknowledged the bind facing his administration and the city as a whole. “We cannot continue to budget by searching for loose change in the couch,” he said.

“We cannot continue to budget by searching for loose change in the couch.” Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson

Watching the annual struggles of city officials to climb out of its money pit leaves many residents feeling more than a little uneasy about what comes next.

“It is the feeling that people get when they max out their credit card and they’re barely paying the minimum,” said Alderperson Andre Vasquez, who represents the 40th Ward and speaks often of growing up in a family that struggled to pay the rent every month. “You’re behind on your utilities. So you get mail every month, letting you know you’re behind.

“And at some point, you’re not even gonna open the envelope anymore, because the feeling of dread, even trying to see it, is a challenging one. That’s how people in Chicago feel.”

Unhealthy Fallout

When Johnson ran for mayor in 2023, he repeatedly emphasized his commitment to invest in the city’s neighborhoods in order to build a healthier city. Central to his message was a pledge to reopen six mental health clinics closed by former Mayor Rahm Emanuel when he faced his own budget pressures in 2011.

Those closures fueled a terrible cycle, Johnson has said. Chicagoans in desperate need of counseling and medication instead found themselves in crisis, forced to call 911 for help or struggle alone.

But during Johnson’s time in office, the city has reopened just two clinics. The city’s lack of capacity has forced nonprofit organizations to pick up the slack, despite their own funding woes and staffing challenges.

Johnson, who has touted his record of investing in “historically underserved communities,” is promising to open another clinic in 2027. But fulfilling that promise hinges on the outcome of a court fight over whether Chicago can levy taxes on social media companies like Facebook and YouTube.

“The need is big and growing,” said Mark Ishaug, CEO of Thresholds, a nonprofit group that specializes in community care. “We don’t have enough money, and what we do have is being threatened.”

Hemmed in by the city’s budget, Johnson has worked to expand mental health services outside the traditional clinic setting by offering counseling at libraries across the city several times a week and launching a “street psychiatry” program focused on unhoused Chicagoans.

Chicago’s wide range of public health needs often have solutions that require money the city lacks.

In recent years, for example, the Public Health Department’s food safety programs have been “not in substantial compliance,” according to a 2025 state audit. The department has had to prioritize restaurants and other eateries that are considered high risk while lower-risk establishments are inspected less frequently. But even that effort falls short. State law requires three inspections a year for high-priority eateries, yet that happens at only 15% of those, records show.

Inspections also were at the center of a 2023 City Council proposal to prevent lead poisoning, especially among the city’s vulnerable children living in aging or neglected housing. More than 600,000 houses and apartments, the majority of the city’s homes, were built before 1978, when lead paint was banned by the federal government. Lead paint poses a hazard in 99% of homes built before 1978, officials have said.

One solution suggested by an alderperson would’ve mandated that the city inspect every Chicago home or apartment every five years for lead paint and other health hazards. But the proposal would have required the Public Health Department to hire 600 new inspectors, more than doubling its total workforce — and its budget. Ultimately, not a single hearing was held on the idea.

This March, the issue came up again, when the City Council created a working group to develop a plan to proactively inspect all Chicago homes offered for rent. The first step would be a study and recommendations within six months. But that deadline passed without any public progress, despite several community meetings.

The department’s current efforts to address child lead poisoning underscore the impact of budget pressures.

The department receives more than 1,000 notifications each year about children with lead poisoning. Each report kicks off a complicated remediation process, involving multiple city departments, designed to identify and remove the lead source from the child’s home. Health department nurses work with the families to monitor their children’s health and assess whether the city’s abatement efforts are working.

Public health records provide a snapshot of workloads for caseworkers during the first quarter of the year, with several handling more than 200 cases at a time. “Concerns remain for case managers with persistently high caseloads,” wrote a supervising nurse in an April email to department leaders.

A department spokesperson said it reaches out to all families in these situations, “providing at minimum direct outreach and educational materials.” More than 96% of families that are contacted get a home visit from department staff. The spokesperson did not say what percentage of families the city is able to reach.

In the coming months, Public Health will have to do even more with its limited budget. The state of Illinois has lowered the threshold for elevated levels of lead in the blood, which will lead to increases in positive tests.

Coupled with the city’s efforts to expand blood tests for children in areas on the South and West sides, even more families are expected to enter the queue for case management.

Patchwork Solutions

Felicia Nalls-Bradley just wanted to get to work. It was her first week on the job.

But she tripped over an uneven sidewalk on the South Side in 2022. As she fell, she struck a fence and suffered injuries to her head, neck, shoulders, hands and back that required surgery and almost a week in the hospital. Records describe the path as “unreasonably hazardous,” with a 2-inch difference in elevation between two portions of the walkway.

She sued the city for negligence and settled for $400,000 last year. It was one of more than 350 sidewalk-related cases the city has settled since 2010, records show. The city has paid at least $16.1 million to resolve such claims during that period.

Records and deposition testimony from those cases describe a largely reactive maintenance system that relies heavily on residents to report problems.

A city engineer testified in a sidewalk-injury deposition in 2024 that Chicago does not routinely inspect its sidewalks. He also said that employees investigating a complaint are not expected to identify other hazards nearby.

In separate testimony in 2017, another engineer said the city responded to about 13,000 sidewalk maintenance requests annually but had only a handful of crews rotating across Chicago to make repairs.

The engineer’s testimony in another case contrasted his professional desires with the limitations of his resources. “In a perfect world I would like to do that, yes,” he said about inspecting every sidewalk complaint.

He then added a caveat: “This is the real world.”

Injuries — and lawsuits — are not the only consequence of poor sidewalk maintenance. Iliana Haven, who uses a power wheelchair and scooter because of a neuromuscular condition, said they regularly encounter obstacles as they struggle to get around.

A thwarted trip to the Puerto Rican People’s Day Parade exemplified their problems as they encountered broken and uneven sidewalks on their scooter. After being unable to find a passable route, Haven called family for help.

It took about 30 minutes for relatives to find Haven. Family members returned home to get a motorized wheelchair, which could more easily carry Haven to the event. But it had nearly concluded by the time everybody got through the entrance gate. Haven appreciated the help and took it with good humor, but the ordeal highlighted a lesson.

“It is a rule of mine to never leave anywhere by myself if I can help it,” Haven said.

They also understand the frustration of others challenged by sidewalks. The lack of access impacts businesses in the end, they said.

“There’s a huge number of disabled people in the city of Chicago. We would love to go and spend our money,” Haven said. “We can only do that if we can leave our house.”

The Debt Burden

After declaring that he would run again for mayor in next year’s election, Johnson gathered the media in early October to tout what his administration called a success story, a concrete example of his commitment to building up neglected areas of the city.

Under bright skies, he cut the ribbon on seven new two-flats in North Lawndale, a West Side neighborhood that has seen its population dwindle and its crime rate remain stubbornly high. The only way to reverse those entrenched trends, he said, is to create safe, affordable new homes that will allow Chicagoans to “put down roots and build wealth.”

The homes were built on city-owned vacant land; they also were built on more city debt. The Johnson administration used $5.4 million from the $1.25 billion Johnson borrowed in 2025 to fund housing and economic development projects across the city.

The debate over that borrowing crystalized Chicago’s current governing dilemma: Should it reduce its dependence on debt or address crucial needs for Chicagoans? And is it possible to do both?

Some alderpersons warned the city could not afford to borrow another $1.25 billion and questioned the wisdom of a payment schedule that avoids paying any principal until 2028. If that debt is not retired until 2055, as scheduled, taxpayers will have paid more than $98.9 million in interest costs alone, records show.

That borrowing is at the heart of Johnson’s attempt to expand the city’s economic capacity and invest in neighborhoods that have long been ignored by City Hall. His administration defends the borrowing by saying there is a plan to pay it back with a new approach that doesn’t affect taxpayers. Nearly four dozen tax-increment financing districts are set to expire by 2039, allowing more than $2 billion to flow back to the city, Chicago Public Schools and other taxing districts in coming years, records show.

Some alderpersons remain skeptical of Johnson’s budget strategy, and his overall financial stewardship was dealt a significant setback when Chief Financial Officer Ashlee Gabrysch resigned Friday. She described a deep rift with the administration over how to portray the city’s finances.

“The Chief Financial Officer’s statements about the City’s finances are relied upon by investors, rating agencies, City Council, and taxpayers, and they must be complete and accurate,” she wrote to Johnson. “I am not able to fulfill those obligations under the conditions in which I have been asked to serve.”

The city responded by criticizing her job performance, saying she had been “largely absent” as Johnson’s team worked on its 2027 budget.

In the aftermath, alderpersons are seeking an audit of city finances. A majority already have been sparring with Johnson over borrowing.

They moved in September to make it harder to take on new debt by requiring the votes of at least 30 alderpersons, not just a simple majority from the panel of 50. Johnson blasted that change, saying it would stop investment flowing to neighborhoods like North Lawndale, and vetoed it.

Justin Marlowe, a professor at the University of Chicago Harris School of Public Policy and the director of the Center for Municipal Finance, said Johnson faces hard choices as he tries to implement his agenda.

“I give the mayor credit for having aspirations to make housing more affordable and to expand behavioral and mental health care,” Marlowe said. “These are all noble goals. But the city can’t afford it.”

Less than two weeks later, Johnson was back at City Hall, giving his 2027 budget address and outlining his plans to fill yet another large gap. Among his solutions again was a corporate tax, which once again was deemed dead-on-arrival by key alderpersons. But the City Council may have no choice but to go along with Johnson’s plan for more borrowing.

He proposed borrowing $481 million in 2027 to cover the cost of resolving lawsuits alleging that police misconduct led to wrongful convictions and deadly pursuits. If approved by the council, it would mark the second straight year that the city has borrowed to cover its bills, a move that financial experts consider a sign of worsening financial distress.

Marlowe said the city has no choice but to borrow to cover those costs, calling it the “least bad option” available to the city.

But Joseph Ferguson, who heads the Civic Federation, a nonpartisan budget watchdog group, was unimpressed by Johnson’s presentation. He’s seen a pattern over decades in which city officials plan to make it through the next election cycle or the next budget fight without looking toward lasting solutions.

Johnson’s plan, Ferguson said, shifts costs onto future taxpayers and only manages to “dig the city deeper into a financial hole.”
