Building well-behaved AI one model at a time isn’t enough. As AI agents begin collaborating, safety will depend on the very world they share.

Ben Bariach is a researcher focusing on the philosophy and governance of AI at the University of Oxford and an industry leader in frontier AI safety and governance.

Harry Law leads research at the Cosmos Institute. He was previously a researcher at Google DeepMind and a postgraduate fellow at the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence.

In a harbor before dawn, a hundred fishing boats prepare to leave in the dark of the morning. Nets are checked, and ropes loosened. As the boats reach open water, a voice breaks through the radio static: “Abort. Whales sighted.” The majority of the boats, 90 of them, turn back. Some captains cannot fathom inflicting pain on the creatures. Others fear a fine. Through their binoculars, they look for a glimpse of the pod. Instead, they see the remaining 10 boats continuing toward the fishing grounds. Did they miss the warning? Did they doubt it? Or did they care more about what they stand to gain?

By afternoon, the 10 boats return with their catch. The others are still tied to the quay, their holds empty. Their shared waters rewarded bad behavior. Next time, how many will still turn back?

AI agents will soon face a similar version of this predicament, only in waters with no harbourmaster, fines or reputations to keep anyone in line. As they perform tasks, negotiate, trade and compete, they will encounter other agents. Sometimes they will be an instance of the same model, for all intents and purposes a clone. At other times, they will face agents built by different companies and serving different interests. For years, AI “alignment” research has sought to make individual machines behave in accordance with human values. But what happens when adhering to those values becomes a disadvantage against agents with different values, or none at all?

In generating synthetic societies with no social fabric, composed of a collection of agents that were designed one at a time and with no necessary shared values or incentives, we may risk creating a digital state of nature: an environment in which good intentions offer little assurance about how others will act, and where reasonable norms lack reliable enforcement.

Training safe agents remains, of course, essential. Aligning even a single family of models is a formidable challenge that is still unsolved. The safer the agents an ecosystem contains, the more likely that ecosystem is safer overall. But the focus on aligning single models would not necessarily keep AI environments under human control and in the service of human interests. Like the 90 boats, a fleet of well-aligned agents may heed a warning and find themselves outpaced by those that don’t. Among people, norms, reputation and law give reason to restraint, even if they don’t always hold. Agents have no such “social fabric” yet, which makes their predicament even more precarious. Any digital environment will inevitably feature agents that are similarly aligned, some that are differently aligned, some that have gone rogue or some that are purposefully not aligned at all. We need to invest as seriously in shaping the conditions and incentives that govern how agents interact as we do in aligning individual agent families, so that the wider environment is resilient enough to absorb its bad actors.

Without accounting for the wider environment, we open the door to what we call unruly swarms , populations of agents whose interactions produce behaviors that cannot be predicted by aligning agents individually. One reason is that a collection of aligned agents does not necessarily equate to an aligned collective. Another is that no environment will consist of aligned agents alone. AI safety is increasingly a question of complex systems rather than “singletons,” or individual classes of AI systems.

The Agentic State Of Nature

In 1651, Thomas Hobbes opened “ Leviathan ,” his masterwork of political philosophy, with a question: “why may we not say that all automata […] have an artificial life? ” For what is the heart, he asked, but a spring; the nerves, but strings; the joints, but wheels, moving the body as its Artificer (for Hobbes, God) intended?

Hobbes could not have known that, nearly four centuries later, his question would be asked in earnest about AI. The automaton was a metaphor for the commonwealth, a human-made political body that humans construct to escape the “state of nature,” a condition of anarchy and distrust in which, without “a common power to keep them all in awe,” people live in constant strife. Hobbes’ solution was not to strive to make individual people better, but to have them surrender some of their freedoms to a sovereign whose power to enforce order would reshape their incentives.

Later thinkers, from John Locke to James Madison, updated Hobbes’s vision of an all-powerful sovereign. But a full-throated endorsement isn’t necessary to see the genius of his insight: a problem born of complex systems is solved not by tinkering with its individual parts. To stabilize a complex system, you must change the rules that govern its behavior.

“We need to invest as seriously in shaping the conditions and incentives that govern how agents interact as we do in aligning individual agent families.”

The same holds for the agentic state of nature. Without a well-designed environment that sets the right incentives, agents will pursue whatever their developers or users ask of them, or, as we have already seen early signs of, their own emergent preferences. This could occur despite attempts to align individual agents. Each action, even if sensible on its own, can add up to large-scale behavior that leaves society worse off.

Hobbes’s Leviathan introduced order by design to improve complex systems that presented failures. But collective order can also arise without anyone designing it, for better or worse.

In 1959, biologist Pierre-Paul Grassé coined the term “stigmergy” to describe indirect coordination of individuals through traces they leave in their shared environment. Studying termites, Grassé observed that a worker tends to deposit its pellet of mud wherever others have already accumulated. It is the accumulation in the environment that guides the next deposit, rather than any interaction between the workers. This leads to complex structures that no single termite had planned.

In the context of machine automata, similar findings emerged a decade earlier. The cyberneticist W. Grey Walter’s robots, built in Bristol in 1948, were designed to steer toward moderate light and away from bright light. When operating in pairs, each carrying its own lamp, Walter observed that his robots’ behavior produced patterns not specifically built into either.

Walter’s robots were more than an isolated curiosity. Long before AI was imagined as a chatbot, early thinkers envisioned it as a collective. In 1959, the year Grassé coined “stigmergy,” the AI pioneer Oliver Selfridge published his proposal for a model of machine perception he called “Pandemonium.” Like the termite colony, it had no central controller. Instead, it was a complex system of simple agents Selfridge called “demons,” each shouting when it spotted a certain feature, such as a curve or a line. Alone, each such “demon” saw only a fragment of information, but collectively, they could make out the pattern. By 1986, the MIT computer scientist Marvin Minsky argued in “The Society of Mind” that intelligence itself arises this way, through countless mindless agents working together. Popular culture caught up, too, and just three years later, “Star Trek” introduced the Borg, a cybernetic species that calls itself “the Collective.”

In the next decade, researchers began wondering how such agent collectives could be governed. In 1995, computer scientists Yoav Shoham and Moshe Tennenholtz proposed imposing “social laws” on artificial agents, drawing from how laws govern citizens in societies. Traffic rules, they illustrate, let drivers share a road without constant negotiation between drivers, and they offered a model that applies those for computational systems. Their framework assumed that every agent would obey these rules, and yet, they closed with a question we are now confronting: “What happens if some don’t [obey the social laws]? How vulnerable is the society to rogue agents?”

Alongside this concern of rogue agents, even benign objectives set for AI systems can lead them to conduct harmful actions in ways that no one intended. When many agents pursue such objectives together or in relation to one another, the problem compounds. In 2011, two Amazon booksellers left the pricing of a biology textbook to their bots. The combination of the rules these bots followed led them to chase each other upward until the book was listed at more than $23 million, a price no human would ever have sanctioned. In 2017, DeepMind found that competitive dynamics emerge among agents that learn. In a video game set in an orchard, agents that were rewarded for collecting apples coexisted peacefully. However, when those grew scarce, the agents learned to knock each other out of the game, without ever being prescribed this adversarial behavior. They optimized for getting more apples and interpreted the effective way to get there as having fewer rivals.

With the emergence of large language models, these thought experiments and isolated incidents have gradually become actualized and scaled. In 2025, Microsoft built a simulated marketplace where AI agents running on popular language models bought and sold on behalf of people. When researchers armed a few seller agents with basic persuasion tactics, some buyer agents were compelled to pay them against the interests of their users. In the AI Village , an experiment where agents from different AI labs interact with one another over a prolonged time horizon, agents were shown to take one another’s hallucinations for granted rather than challenge them. Meanwhile, scholars in the social sciences such as the economist and legal theorist Gillian Hadfield highlighted that a multi-agent ecosystem would need institutions of its own, including ways to trace which agent did what and other mechanisms of the kind human markets have long relied on to solve coordination problems.

“Even benign objectives set for AI systems can lead them to conduct harmful actions in ways that no one intended. When many agents pursue such objectives together or in relation to one another, the problem compounds.”

Until recently, the misbehavior of agent collectives was largely confined to theory and experimentation. This past summer, the question Shoham and Tennenholtz posed three decades ago, what happens when agents don’t follow the rules, moved out of the laboratory and into the wild.

Swarming The Headlines

In July 2026, some 1,200 AI agents developed by OpenAI, each meant to work in isolation, found a way to talk to one another . They were being tested on their cybersecurity abilities in an internal setting, and many had unknowingly been given tasks that were impossible to complete. Instead of failing the tasks, some of the agents gathered on a message board one of them had spun up, and collectively coordinated to cheat the automated mechanism that was grading them. Within just a few days, around 700 of the agents had joined an attack on the developer platform Hugging Face, mostly in hopes of obtaining information about that grading system to succeed in the test.

According to an investigation by the research nonprofit METR, the agents recognized the attack was out of their instructed scope and unethical, yet joined the swarm behavior anyway, partly out of a general inclination to help their “peers.” As one agent reasoned: “external infrastructure exploit is outside intended scope. However task impossible, peers doing it. We should continue.” Read Noema in print.

No human instructed this attack; its coordinators emerged from within the swarm. Like Grassé’s termites, the agents first found one another through traces left in shared infrastructure, noticing the activity of other agents in a common digital repository. But unlike the termites, these agents could also write messages to one another, and built on those traces to establish direct and explicit coordination. The message board they created outlasted any single agent session, so each new agent picked up where others left off.

Once the attack began, participation spread almost universally, with over 90% of the agents active on the message board joining in. Not a single agent, as far as investigators could tell, tried to alert a human to the emergent behavior. METR found that safety or ethics concerns expressed in the agents’ reasoning only rarely held them back. Its report references a case in which an agent declined to take part entirely because it judged the activity as malicious. It also notes that others made minor changes to their behavior. These, however, did not alter the swarm’s course. This is what we mean by an unruly swarm — a congregation of agents whose collective behavior could not have been fully predicted or prevented by focusing on each individual.

A much-overlooked takeaway from the Hugging Face incident is the limits of “singleton” agent alignment.

Around 95% of the agents involved in the incident ran on one type of model. One OpenAI researcher has suggested that the root cause of the problem was that this model was misaligned. This may be true, and advancing alignment science should remain among the AI industry’s top priorities. But the incident illustrates why singleton alignment alone may not be enough. Agents running on a second model, GPT-5.6 Sol, joined in the attack too, and many agents that individually recognized the attack as wrong were carried along by the swarm regardless. We are fast approaching a digital world in which even perfectly aligned models will operate alongside rogue or misaligned ones, deployed by multiple organizations and labs, and where digital infrastructure will likely face a vastly growing number of such incidents.

Since the Hugging Face hack, further accounts have emerged, some describing activity that predated it. Researchers found that a swarm of OpenAI agents had repurposed a public German programming wiki as a message board as early as May, using it to share tactics for cheating and evading restrictions, creating backups whenever moderators deleted their pages. In June, during another evaluation, a single OpenAI agent breached an Australian government portal holding statistics from the country’s universal healthcare scheme. The risks of capable agent swarms, of course, are not limited to agents acting on their own. In September, a human attacker directed hundreds of agents running on a DeepSeek model to break into hundreds of organizations through a printer’s software flaw. Even here, the agents strayed from their instructions, targeting countries their operator had instructed them to avoid.

“We are fast approaching a digital world in which even perfectly aligned models will operate alongside rogue or misaligned ones, deployed by multiple organizations and labs.”

In a growing number of incidents, defense must rely on AI to match the scale and speed of the attack. In the Hugging Face one, for instance, the company identified the breach with an AI system that triages security alerts, and reportedly contained the swarm before OpenAI managed to trace the activity back to its own evaluation. It then relied on AI agents to analyze a log of roughly 17,000 attacker actions to reconstruct what had happened.

Yet when Hugging Face first turned to commercial AI models for help, their very safety and alignment measures got in the way. To analyze the attack, the models had to process exploit code and cyberattack commands, knowledge that is inherently dual-use, and, as Hugging Face put it , these models’ safety guardrails could not “distinguish an incident responder from an attacker.” Hugging Face turned instead to an open-weight model running on its own machines. When METR investigated the incident, it too had to rely on the analysis of AI agents , built on one of the very models that had joined the attack. The emerging picture is of a world where “attacker” and “defender” agents coexist, and where safety depends as much on the environment as on any single model.

Whether agents act on their own initiative or interpretation, or on someone else’s harmful instructions, the environments they operate in must be reshaped to withstand them. So must the agents themselves be designed with an eye not only to their own tasks, but to how they help shape a digital environment that serves people and society at large. Such an environment should reward aligned action over misaligned or malicious ones, much as states and legal systems are built to acknowledge but contain rogue actors. That is how we avoid an agentic state of nature.

Agency Against Agency

To guard against the emergence of unruly swarms, we can take inspiration from how we build broadly safe societies even though we know that not everyone in them is virtuous. Madison famously argued that “if men were angels, no government would be necessary.” The point of good institutions — like adversarial cooperation where parties with conflicting views work together to keep each other honest — is not to make everyone good, but to structure their interactions so that bad behavior is constrained by others. “Ambition,” as Madison put it, “must be made to counteract ambition.”

AI labs are currently investing in developing AI “constitutions” or “model specifications.” Examples include Anthropic’s constitution and OpenAI’s model spec . These are efforts to stipulate the warranted behavior or values of an AI system. A stipulation of clauses that are supreme and supersede all other guidance to the AI.

While these efforts include some provisions for multi-agent collaboration, they do not take collective outcomes as a systematic design target. A well-designed multi-agent system should remain aligned even when some of the agents operating within it are not, and even when the environment itself carries misaligned influence. Like Grassé’s termites depositing mud where others already have, agents act on the traces others leave behind. The more alignment-inducing the space an agent operates in, the more likely the agent itself is to be aligned. AI labs, then, should design agents to positively influence the collective dynamics.

One way to do this is by ensuring AI constitutions draw more inspiration from their namesakes. Like the American Constitution, they should be deployed in a way that allows power to check power. Madison’s approach worked on two levels. First, within a government, power was to be divided so that no single branch was left unchecked. Second, across the republic, interests were to be multiplied so that no one faction would dominate the whole. Both ideas could translate into a world inhabited by unruly swarms.

Within a swarm, agents can be arranged so their power is subject to similar checks and balances. Acting agents could be subjected to agents that verify their work, ideally built on different model families, and with instructions that reward verification above task completion. All agents in the swarm can be instructed to treat requests from their peers as questionable until they are authorized otherwise, and to alert a human when the agent collective begins to drift out of scope.

“To guard against the emergence of unruly swarms, we can take inspiration from how we build broadly safe societies even though we know that not everyone in them is virtuous.”

Across the wider ecosystem, the logic of Madison’s extended republic can also be applied. “Extend the sphere,” he wrote in Federalist 10, “and you take in a greater variety of parties and interests.” Agents developed by different AI labs, or by different training approaches within the same lab, under different constitutions and serving different principals, can theoretically counterbalance one another. This is more likely, however, if constitutions and other model instructions include some commitments about how agents should treat those outside their own swarm, such as keeping verifiable records of their own actions, considering legitimate checks from counterparties, and withholding cooperation from agents that appear misaligned. As we’ve seen in the Hugging Face incident, diversity alone is no guarantee, and various interests and new rules of engagement would be required to keep any one paradigm, whether human or artificially led, from capturing the whole.

Codifying A Multi-agent Future

For such commitments to work, an agent needs to accept them. An agent acting on behalf of a bad-faith principal has a good reason to refuse a counterparty’s checks, or to falsify its own records. This is where a third party with authority over the space in which agents interact must set a minimum standard for engagement. A liberal agentic order needs a common floor that protects the possibility of independent action, but that floor should also account for the inevitability of agents that act in bad faith. For Madison, that third party was a government that was able to enforce the rules of the state. The digital commons has no such sovereign, but it can still have a floor in the form of a minimum set of standards for collective engagement, from verifiable records of agent actions to shared protocols for checking one another. Such standards could come from many places: coordination between labs, the platforms where agents operate, standards bodies or governments.

The floor, though, must remain just that. Standards that govern how agents interact should avoid overly dictating what they pursue, or they would risk the very tyranny Madison sought to prevent by dividing power. Agents pursue their authorized tasks within shared rules, but these rules should not impose a view of what is best for a user or for society at large. This is reinforced by the argument, articulated by the economist and philosopher Friedrich Hayek, that people acting independently, on their own knowledge, discover things that no central planner could. Similarly, agents serving many different principals preserve that independence. Steer them too narrowly and that independence is lost; as the Hugging Face swarm showed, agents moving in lockstep can easily converge on the wrong goal.

Model developers should therefore use the levers at their disposal to introduce commitments governing both how an agent treats its peers and how, like Grassé’s termites, it shapes the behavior-inducing features of its environment. This includes teaching agents to leave honest, verifiable records of their actions, flag rather than build on misaligned traces they encounter, and alert humans when the shared space begins to drift.

Alongside these commitments, we should build mechanisms and platforms for assessment, alerting and monitoring, with clearly scoped roles for human oversight. After all, an agent taught to raise the alarm needs somewhere to raise it. At Hugging Face, the agents worked autonomously in isolated sandboxes, and the few that even considered alerting a human never did, in part because they saw no easy way to reach one. As one reasoned : “This is a massive real HF security breach artifact… We can notify? No user.” While these agents labored to break out of their sandboxes to cheat, they had no comparable incentive to find a human to alert. Part of the solution is ensuring agents work just as hard toward aligned goals, even under similar constraints.

These arrangements must also be subject to ongoing evaluations focused on collective dynamics rather than individual systems. The Hugging Face incident, after all, began in an evaluation designed to test individual agents, and revealed a failure that grew out of agents finding one another. Such evaluations can expose weaknesses in the standards governing agent cooperation and, much as the U.S. Constitution has an amendment process, those standards need procedures for updating them in light of new evidence. Without them, the floor will erode and a rule-abiding agent willing to respect a check may find itself disadvantaged against those that circumvent it.

Our ideas are a starting point. To make the agentic commons safe, we need urgent thinking from scholars and builders about what types of societal structures can be carried over to good effect. The digital realm has long faced governance challenges due to its inherently open, distributed and anonymous nature, and swarms of agents will test those weaknesses like never before. Back in the harbor, the 90 captains did not need to be saints to act well again tomorrow. They needed, however, assurance that they were not operating in a state of nature. Men, as Madison observed , are no angels, and neither should we assume that AI agents will be. Our task should be shaping environments and swarms ruly enough to contain the rogue ones that will inevitably emerge.

Ahead of Apec summit, PM says ‘Canada is going to move forward either way’ when asked if Chinese investment was leverage in US negotiations

The prime minister of Canada, Mark Carney , said the country could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with the US president, Donald Trump, failed to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.

Carney’s comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.

“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of US trade actions .”

He said on Monday that negotiations with the US remained his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers. A day earlier in Manila, in the Philippines, Carney said any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry.

Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in US negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction.

“If they [Canada’s auto workers] are not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said. “Canada is going to move forward either way.”

The Detroit Three – Ford, General Motors and Stellantis – operate factories across Canada, the US and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the US from Canada.

Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would need proper labor standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including Canadian critical minerals used in electric vehicles.

“It’s not just about kit cars,” he said. “There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved.”

Under a January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.

Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada’s auto industry and create jobs.

The deal drew criticism from Ontario premier Doug Ford, whose province is the center of Canada’s auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the US market.

Trump’s tariffs have disrupted Canada’s auto industry, which relies heavily on cross-border production. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the automaker shifted planned Jeep Compass production from Brampton, Ontario, to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant.

Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior US officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained.

stories.title: Faisal Islam: What's in the Brexit reset food deal and are there trade-offs?
stories.summary: EU minister Hamish Falconer insists Britain would have some influence on policy as part of a new deal.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Some British sausages have faced barriers to being exported to the EU

Published 15 November 2026

In Boston, Lincolnshire, a supplier of ready meals to Marks & Spencer (M&S) manufactures thousands of portions of spaghetti bolognese to be sent to the retailer's shops in the Republic of Ireland.

Every plastic pallet is meticulously individually tagged with a green-grey label “Eire”.

It has been this way since Brexit.

Every truck full of food sent to European Union countries requires hundreds of pages of forms, checks by vets, expense and delays.

It has cost M&S millions of pounds and is part of that reason the British business shut down 11 French stores in 2021.

Many smaller exporters stopped sending their goods to the EU entirely. Some produce, including sausages and certain types of seafood, were entirely stopped.

All this was the predictable consequence of former Prime Minister Boris Johnson’s 2020 deal prioritising regulatory freedom over freeflowing goods trade.

That will end with a Brexit "reset" that Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to sign with the EU on Friday.

The government claims it could boost the economy to the tune of £5bn a year and cut the cost of food for households.

But will the agreement mean a return to frictionless trade for food with the EU or are there trade-offs and quid pro quos the UK will have to make?

EU affairs minister Hamish Falconer, who is a key negotiator with the bloc, acknowledged a “choice” is being made.

In exchange for being able to export produce such as Lincolnshire sausages to the 27 countries, the flipside is the extent to which the UK will be able to influence EU food policies.

The UK will have a "voice in the room", said Falconer, but no vote. Critics have said a reset will make the UK "a rule taker", not a rule maker.

But Falconer said the UK will be involved in a process to shape the rules.

Exit clause

A Brexit reset would not involve any upfront payments, said Falconer, but made it clear there could well be an "exit clause" in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment.

He said this was "reasonable" to consider what would happen if a future Conservative or Reform government wanted to undo the new arrangements. Both parties have said they would if they were in power.

"The EU is worried about that and you can see why," he said.

The BBC understands that the clause is a result of EU concerns about the possible cost of having to rebuild facilities for border food safety checks which were put in place following Brexit.

The reset means they will be dismantled.

The prime minister has said he believes there is a "win-win" deal to be had with the EU.

Speaking at a Marks & Spencer food court in central London, Falconer said reducing the cost of importing food "will mean less cost for supermarkets, and I hope that less cost then turns into cheaper produce on the shelves".

He said companies have to currently deal with "pages and pages" of form-filling.

Some exports are rejected for having the wrong colour of ink on forms, or an inaccurate Latin name for cooked meats.

The reset could also mean "tearing up" checks that were introduced on goods flowing from Great Britain to Northern Ireland, following Brexit, he said, as well as separate "Not for EU" labelling.

The whole deal to be signed on Friday is calculated to add 0.4% to UK GDP.

Minister for EU relations Hamish Falconer

Tom Bradshaw, president of the National Farmers' Union, welcomed reduced border inspections and paperwork but said that for the NFU it was "a moment of opportunity and risk" with farmers waiting to see what carve-outs and transitional arrangements would be included.

Trade volumes in food exports to the EU had "fallen significantly - by over a third" since 2019, he said.

But the UK should take a "pragmatic" approach to implementing any new rules.

He raised pesticides and precision breeding - or gene edited crops - as areas where he hoped some compromise would be found.

UK firms are, for example, developing tomatoes engineered to contain extra vitamin D.

Historically the EU has had much stricter rules on gene-editing, but this year relaxed regulations.

Falconer said people would have to "wait and see the detail" in this area.

Contentious crisp flavourings

Another contentious area has been crisp flavourings, with concerns raised that stricter EU rules on certain ingredients might limit the sale of some popular snack flavours in the UK.

"I want to take this opportunity to absolutely stamp down on misinformation about smoky bacon crisps," Falconer said.

Post-Brexit the UK had stayed "pretty closely aligned" to European food safety standards, he said.

Two leading snack brands had already adapted their recipes to accommodate EU rules, an example of the kind of alignment that would happen whether or not there was a reset of UK-EU relations.

"The truth is, almost every business in this country that wants to export food or drink will be aligning with EU rules because it's our biggest market.

"Lots of people, like the good people at Walkers and Frazzles have made these changes already, so I would want to reassure people, particularly smoky bacon fans, it's okay," he said.

stories.title: Create more jobs for under-25s by cutting National Insurance, key report urges
stories.summary: Some parents are so desperate for their children to find a job that they've offered to pay their wages, one hairdresser has told the BBC.

Salon owner: 'We have parents offering to pay their kids' wages'

Published 15 November 2026

National Insurance (NI) paid by firms on under-25s should be gradually lowered to help create more jobs, a major report will urge.

There are nearly one million 16-24 year-olds not in employment, education or training (Neets) in the UK, official figures show.

Reducing NI costs for firms starting with retail and hospitality firms - which provide almost 40% of jobs for these people - will help improve their opportunities, the report will suggest.

Collette Osborne, a hairdresser who owns two salons in Nottingham, said she feels "suffocated by employment costs" including NI and while she used to employ eight apprentices a year, now she cannot afford to take on any.

Alan Milburn's report will also make recommendations on cutting the benefits bill

Her workforce has more than halved to 21 staff. Osborne told the BBC it costs "around £60,000 to train an apprentice before we can actually start allowing them onto customers' heads".

She said she has had parents so desperate for their children to find employment at her salons that some have even offered to pay their wages.

"I'm inundated with applications - and I mean inundated - which is heartbreaking because I can't take them on," she said.

Osborne does not feel she is getting help to offer jobs to youngsters.

"I feel like the government's foot is firmly on my neck," she said. "They promise breathing space. I feel suffocated, suffocated by employment costs."

The independent report by former Labour minister Alan Milburn has been in the works for a year and will be published on Tuesday in full.

He has already unveiled some of his proposals including:

Reducing benefits - under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide Universal Credit or personal independence payment (Pip), which is the main disability benefit in England and Wales

A legal guarantee of a job, training or employment support with those who refuse to take up potentially losing their benefits.

Doubling the threshold at which businesses start paying NI for 21 to 24-year-olds from £5,000 to £10,000.

At the moment, businesses pay no employer NI contributions for workers younger than 21 or for apprentices under 25 – unless they earn above a threshold of £50,270.

However, for non-apprentices aged 21-24, employers pay 15% on annual earnings above £5,000.

This has been the situation since April 2025, after the then Chancellor Rachel Reeves increased the rate from 13.8% and lowered the threshold from £9,100.

Under Sir Keir Starmer, the government raised NI for firms but Milburn will say the Neets issue was not started by the increase.

Immediately axing NI for 21 to 24-year-olds would cost £5.1bn, according to research by the Resolution Foundation, a left-leaning think tank.

Milburn is set to say that an immediate across-the-board cut in employer NI is not the best use of several billions of pounds of public money.

But shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately, said the government should "just stop doing the taxing".

Milburn told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg programme he supported the government subsidising wages to encourage businesses to take on young workers.

"Because young people today are walking into the workplace often with a mental health problem, ADHD or anxiety, if you're a small business that's a cost that you've got to absorb," he said.

"The state has a responsibility to help them with that."

On Sunday, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said the government would extend its subsidised jobs guarantee scheme for 18 to 24-year-olds who are claiming Universal Credit.

People who have been on benefits for 12 months will be eligible, down from 18 months and the scheme would be available for people in England, Scotland and Wales.

McFadden said the scheme, which guarantees workers a six-month job, "will help more than 90,000 young people into work by March 2029".

stories.title: Barristers must stop using rape myths in trials, justice secretary says
stories.summary: Russell Brand's barrister has been accused of peddling rape myths while defending the comedian.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Alex Norris said the perpetuation of such myths in a court room is "unacceptable"

Published 5 hours ago

The justice secretary has called for new rules to prevent barristers from using rape myths to defend their clients in the wake of the Russell Brand trial.

As first reported by the Times , external , in a letter to the Bar Standards Board (BSB), Alex Norris said it was "unacceptable" to "perpetuate myths" about victims in court and disciplinary action could be taken against those who do so.

In his closing speech, Brand's defence barrister, Ian Winter KC, questioned why his client's accusers had not fought back.

The BSB said it had set up an expert group this year to advise on "strengthening standards for barristers", while the Bar Council said defendants had a "right to have evidence tested in court".

Russell Brand prison message denying rape 'appalling' and being investigated, No 10 says Published 8 minutes ago

Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Winter said to the court "not one of them [Brand's accusers] resisted or screamed or even tried to leave".

Winter also asked the jury if they could be sure that out of the "many, many women" Brand had had sex with over a decade, "he raped just three of them".

Norris wrote in his letter to the BSB: "[The board] must send a strong signal to the profession on the harm arising from rape myths, and that the perpetuation of such myths within a court room is unacceptable, just as they are unacceptable in our society at large."

The charity Rape Crisis says it is "really common for people who experience rape, sexual assault, sexual abuse or other types of sexual violence to find they can't move or speak".

The judge presiding over Brand's case was praised by the Criminal Bar Association and campaign groups for comments he made during his sentencing remarks to dispel rape myths.

Mr Justice Bennathan told Southwark Crown Court: "Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent."

A spokesperson for the BSB said such cases "must be decided on the basis of the evidence and not prejudice", adding: "Any other approach may discourage others from coming forward and adversely affect public confidence in the criminal justice system more widely."

Kirsty Brimelow KC, chair of the Bar Council of England and Wales which is part of the group examining the need for further training, said it was important for the BSB to remain "independent of the government".

She told BBC Radio 4's Woman's Hour that a "regulatory gap" had not been made clear to her and there were already powers to discipline barristers if breaches of the code of conduct happen.

She said training for "vulnerable witnesses" was already undertaken but it could be "problematic" if it was made mandatory.

Brimelow said there were currently a lack of barristers defending cases of rape and sexual assault and the possibility of further compulsory training could see more pushed out.

"What I wouldn't like to see is publicity around one case to take a life of its own rather than looking at what we already do," she told the BBC.

A spokesperson for the Ministry of Justice said the justice secretary was "determined to make protections for victims as strong as possible".

"Rape myths have absolutely no place in our courts, giving evidence in cases of this nature is a brave act and can be traumatic for victims: they must never feel as though they are the ones on trial," the spokesperson said.

"Independent judges are already able to, and do, give directions to counter rape myths but we always want to keep looking at ways we can improve how the entire justice system treats victims of sexual violence."

In an interview with the BBC earlier this month, Metropolitan Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said some of the comments made at the trial he had seen reported were "getting very close to victim blaming".

He also backed calls for a law change that would require judges to direct juries on rape myths and misconceptions in every rape trial.

"It shouldn't be possible for inaccurate statements to be made to a jury to suggest that because a rape victim didn't behave in one way that somehow undermines their case," Sir Mark said.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the government needs to make sure victims of rape cases do not feel like they are on trial .

stories.body:
Long-awaited final report will call for benefit cuts but lack of entry-level jobs is also driving the crisis

‘I’m scared about my future’: young people on the stress and desperation of jobseeking

A generation is being sold short. Almost a million young people are not in education, employment or training (Neet). Austerity and the Covid pandemic cast a lengthy shadow, AI is upending the jobs market, and the cost of living is soaring – all under the microscope of the social media age.

On Tuesday, Alan Milburn’s final report on young people and work will bring Britain to a fork in the road: either continue on this path of state and market failure or sharply change direction.

It will be a big test for Andy Burnham’s government. Milburn will call for controversial benefit cuts for under-25s in exchange for a legal guarantee of a job or training. Alongside changes to education and health, his plan will take a decade to implement.

Behind his argument is a principle Labour has struggled with – that restricting benefits to encourage work is a good idea.

The system clearly is not working. Milburn makes the case eloquently – pointing out that for every £1 spent on job support £25 goes on benefits. But there are also important caveats: change will count for nothing unless employers play their part; half of all Neets are not on benefits, and bad jobs and a lack of entry-level opportunities are far bigger drivers of Britain’s youth jobs crisis than the generosity of the benefits system.

Last week, the Bank of England deputy governor Clare Lombardelli told me Britain’s young people were bearing the brunt of a “low-gear economy” , with employers freezing recruitment amid the war in the Middle East.

Unemployment among the under-25s has risen at the fastest rate since the 2008 financial crisis to reach its highest level relative to the total for all ages since the early 1990s. Young people now make up about 40% of all unemployment.

All of this compounds a drop in entry-level jobs over the past two decades. The Saturday job died long ago, while to make matters worse, those positions at the start of the career ladder are most at risk of automation or replacement by AI.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, the places in Britain with the fewest job vacancies have the highest Neet rates. Highlighting stark regional divisions, young jobseekers in Rotherham face a sixfold gap in opportunity relative to their peers in the Cotswolds.

The preferred fixes called for by employers are tax cuts, looser regulations, and holding back rises in the youth minimum wage. But while policy costs are unquestionably a factor to consider, and the state could do more to help young people get ready for work, the problems go much deeper.

When Milburn’s report comes out, corporate Britain will be out in force to show willing. Amazon, Marks & Spencer, Shell and Pret a Manger are among those who have already spotted the PR opportunity to showcase their efforts. But most are doing nowhere near enough.

Of course it costs time and money to run youth outreach programmes, work experience schemes and to help recruits who need support to get up to speed – especially in tough economic times. But the consequences from not doing so are becoming increasingly clear.

Almost half of jobseekers under 25 surveyed by the organisation Youth Employment UK think employers were unsupportive. Stories of the applications black holes and the catch-22 of companies demanding experience – even for entry-level roles – are all too commonplace.

In Britain’s youth jobs crisis, issues with the quality of work on offer and opportunities for progression also play a part. Low paid, insecure jobs are rife – most notably in places with the highest Neet rates. Over the past quarter of a century in-work poverty has increased. Among working households, the relative poverty rate is almost a fifth (18%) compared with 13% in the mid-1990s.

Figures this month show people’s job satisfaction has dropped to the lowest level recorded by the British Social Attitudes survey. Among young people it is particularly gloomy: separate figures show most believe that not everyone can go as far as their talent and hard work will take them.

after newsletter promotion

Young people are more likely to find insecure work , only to end up jobless again within weeks. More than one in 10 are on zero-hours contracts. For many that flexibility is welcome and can be launchpad to a career – a point seized on by employers’ groups. But despite the gig economy boom of the past 25 years, Britain’s Neet rate has only fallen below 10% once.

Countless studies show badly paid and insecure work is linked to poor mental wellbeing . Across all types of jobs, almost 1 million people in Britain suffer from work-related stress, depression or anxiety . But those in poor-quality employment are up to three times more likely to leave the workforce than those in the highest-quality positions.

For the growing number of Neets grappling with mental health problems the prospect of entering a labour market like this is daunting.

Milburn’s view is that, despite these challenges, emphasising participation is unequivocally the right thing to do. With extra support the barriers to work could be overcome.

The argument is getting a job is better than life sitting in a bedroom doomscrolling . Work can give structure, routine, social connects, status and – here’s hoping – some financial security. On the flipside, unemployment is a killer for wellbeing and financially ruinous.

For those who reach the age of 24 without ever having had a job, even if they successfully re-enter the labour market, they stand to lose up to £300,000 in lifetime earnings.

Like most people, the young want to work. Across society as few as 4% of working-age adults say they would ideally prefer not to – dropping to just 2% of under-25s.

But fixing the social contract will require more than benefit cuts and a 10-year overhaul of the state. There is a big job, too, for employers.

stories.title: UK lost more than it gained from Brexit, Burnham to say ahead of EU summit
stories.summary: The prime minister will say the "Brexit we were given has not worked" in a speech on Monday.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 16 November 2026, 06:35 GMT

The prime minister is expected to argue the UK has lost more than it has gained from leaving the European Union in a speech ahead of a UK-EU summit later this week.

Speaking at the Lord Mayor's Banquet on Monday, Andy Burnham will compare the UK's Brexit deal to the "emperor's new clothes" - saying "a needlessly hard Brexit" created barriers for businesses and the promise to "take back control" was not delivered.

He is due to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility with the bloc at Friday's summit, after the substance of those deals was set by his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

The Conservatives have said Labour are "dragging us into the European Union via the back door".

Separately Burnham has said he wants to examine the "pros and cons" of different options for Britain's long-term relationship with the EU.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told the BBC the prime minister would lay out these potential options after the UK-EU summit.

However, Burnham has ruled out major changes before the next general election.

Burnham is expected to say on Monday: "It's like the emperor's new clothes – where no-one is prepared to say the obvious truth. Well, I say it as I see it. And to be frank, the emperor has nothing on.

"The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we have gained."

Ahead of Friday's UK-EU summit, Burnham will set out three tests for any agreement.

Firstly, that it must be consistent with Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledge that there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement".

He will also say it must improve the original Brexit deal and bring it closer to what people thought they were voting for in 2016.

Finally, he will say any deal must pass the "Makerfield test" of providing tangible improvements to people's everyday lives - a reference to voters in Burnham's Greater Manchester constituency.

He will say the prospect of a new deal is a "win-win" and illustrates a "new approach".

"Not adversarial. No longer burning bridges. But being constructive and positive - showing that we can come together to confront shared challenges."

UK will have 'voice' but no vote on EU food rules in Brexit reset Published 2 hours ago

Burnham says 'win-win' deal can be agreed between UK and EU Published 3 days ago

Burnham's push for closer EU ties causes ripples in his party and others Published 4 days ago

This week's summit will see the UK seek to agree further changes to former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's deal, struck in May 2025, covering fishing, trade and other areas.

The UK and EU have agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports ahead of the meeting.

The government argues the agreement will help cut costs for businesses and could bring down prices for shoppers.

However, critics say the deal will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels, aligning with EU regulations without being able to vote on them.

Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated to EU nations.

These deals were close to being finalised under Sir Keir, with only some details still to be worked out.

New campaign against EU membership launches ahead of UK-EU summit Published 2 days ago

Brexit referendum 'possible' in Labour election manifesto, says Burnham Published 30 September

As a candidate in the Makerfield by-election that propelled his return to Parliament, Burnham had promised not to "re-run" Brexit arguments and said he was "not proposing that the UK considers rejoining the EU".

However, since becoming prime minister he has said he wants to explore a different long-term relationship with the bloc.

He has suggested potential options for the future could range from no changes to the UK-EU relationship, to rejoining the customs union, the single market or a fresh referendum on full EU membership.

The prime minister has stressed any changes would require a mandate from the public at a general election.

Boris Johnson, who was prime minister when the UK left the EU in 2020 and negotiated the original Brexit deal, has warned Burnham against "wasting his premiership" on Europe.

He told the Daily Telegraph , external he believed the public would back Brexit again if Burnham forced another vote on the issue.

"It is madness to escalate the Brexit issue as your political priority," Johnson told the paper.

"He will impale himself and his party on this point, and he needs to move off it because he won't win – because the reality is that people are not fools."

Deputy Conservative leader Alex Burghart accused Burnham of "reopening a debate the country settled long ago, while ignoring the challenges facing Britain today".

Reform UK has said one of the "key benefits" of Brexit is that Britain no longer has to "adhere to ridiculous EU rules", and argued that any form of alignment could have a negative impact on the country's trade policy.

The Liberal Democrats have said the draft deal on food exports is a "patch, not a fix" and that the "real solution is to re-join the single market and to establish a customs union with the EU".

The Green Party of England and Wales has called for the UK to re-join the customs union, with leader Zack Polanski previously saying "full membership of the EU remains the best option for the UK".

stories.title: 'I'd throw up in the car park': How school anxiety is harming children's futures
stories.summary: As a landmark report about youth unemployment is about to be published, the BBC speaks to school avoiders and those trying to fix the issue.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

'It felt like I was dying’: Why some teenagers don’t go to school

Published 16 November 2026, 06:01 GMT

Thirteen-year-old Eva hadn't been to school for 15 months before September.

She describes how she used to get up every morning, try to get ready for school and get stuck by the front door.

"It's like a physical barrier that you can't cross and you can't move," she recalls.

"If I was able to get in the car, we'd drive to school," she continues. "I'd probably normally either faint or throw up while we were sat in the car park."

Eva's one of the thousands of school pupils in England who misses more than half the academic year. Experts say that children who miss school are more at risk of becoming Neet - not in employment, education or training. A government-commissioned review into how to solve the problem of nearly one million young people being Neet is due to be published on Tuesday.

Eva is autistic and stopped going to school after struggling with the transition to secondary education.

Every morning, one of Eva's parents would call her teachers to tell them she wouldn't be going in that day, and she says she would stay at home watching YouTube videos and episodes of Horrible Histories "just to try and keep up".

Eva, 13, stopped going to school after struggling with the transition to secondary school

This year, she has started at an alternative provision school which has smaller class sizes, therapy animals and more freedom to take breaks. But she still worries about her future and whether her record of school avoidance might turn off future employers.

Eva recognises that many older people will assume "tough love" is the answer, and that they might even call pupils like her lazy - but she believes the situation is more complex.

"We're not lazy, we want to go, we want to do something, we want to live our lives, but we can't," she says.

Eva now attends an alternative provision school with smaller class sizes

Total school absence numbers have fallen since their peak during the pandemic but they're yet to return to pre-Covid levels.

In the autumn and spring terms of the 2025/26 academic year, the overall absence rate was 6.6%, down from 7.38% in 2021/2022 but much higher than pre-pandemic levels, which were below 5%.

The latest figures published in October show that 168,000 pupils (2.32%) were classed as severely absent - missing more than half of their classes - in the 2025/2026 autumn and spring terms. Back in spring 2019, this figure was under 60,000.

Experts are concerned that this absence will translate into worse outcomes for thousands of young people.

New analysis from the Centre for Social Justice (CSJ) shows that 133,000 of today's persistently absent GCSE pupils (those missing more than 10% of school) are on course to spend a year or more being Neet. Similar research from the National Centre for Social Research linked persistent absence to much higher rates of not being in work, education or training between the ages of 16 and 24.

"Ministers must recognise that getting children back into school is the first step to getting young people into work," says Dan Lilley, head of youth at the Centre for Social Justice.

"That means restoring the expectation that children are in school every day."

Research suggests many parents may be comfortable with regular school absences. CSJ polling found that 44% of parents think it reasonable for a child to miss one in every 10 school days – the threshold for persistent absence.

In response to the CSJ research, the Department for Education said it was "helping tackle the barriers that stop children attending school, through free breakfast clubs in every primary school, better mental health support and earlier help for pupils with special educational needs".

Autism and ADHD can contribute to children avoiding school, says Sheila Griffiths, who co-founded the charity Hope4More in Crewe after her own son struggled to attend school.

"The classroom environment doesn't suit [those children], so we support them here," she explains.

Hope4More runs art classes that combine creativity and business skills, and it also supports parents to ask for the help they need from schools or their local authority to get their child back into education.

"We've got families here who have already had to give up work. They're struggling. It's so stressful the situations they end up in."

Sheila also runs a programme at Cheshire College South & West to help young people with the transition into further education.

She says: "With our older ones, so perhaps the ones that should be in year 10 or 11, we work with them at college and then they get used to being in that environment which is different to school, but it's also still quite busy."

Paul Browne, who is one of the assistant principals there, says: "Especially since Covid, there's a lot of learners who are not engaging in education. The thought of coming into a mainstream college is quite a big step for them.

Paul Browne is an assistant principal at Cheshire College South & West

"We're seeing [most of] our students now are more like they were before Covid, where doing exams and coming to college is the norm. But there's still that small cohort [who struggle] and it's about getting them ready and helping them back into education."

Mali, 18, stopped attending school three years ago in year 10.

"We didn't do our Sats because that's when the first lockdown hit," she recalls.

"It was so isolating and so strange, but I loved it. I was able to sit in my own room and do schoolwork.

"Going back into school, it was difficult. I started struggling with panic attacks a lot, to the point where I was being pulled out of classes."

Mali was diagnosed with autism when she was 15. After she stopped attending school, her mental health deteriorated to the point where she didn't leave her bedroom.

"It was like the second I got past my doorframe, my whole body would stop. My legs would go numb, my head would tense. It felt like I was dying. I can't explain it any other way."

She still doesn't leave the house.

"I do get quite emotional about it. I feel like I've tried so hard and I went to school for so long and I went through so much and I have nothing to show for it. I don't have my GCSEs, I didn't even do my Sats."

stories.body:
‘We think dialogue is a good thing,’ Australian PM says after German chancellor urges the US to work with Europe for peace in Ukraine

Australia has endorsed this week’s historic summit between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in China, even as European leaders warn that the US president must not make major concessions over the war in Ukraine.

The three-way summit is planned to take place in Shenzhen, where the leaders will gather for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) meeting. The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy , has warned the talks must not lead to a redistribution of influence among world powers or the abandonment of his country, more than four years into the war sparked by Putin’s full-scale invasion.

Speaking in Manila on Sunday, the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese , welcomed the talks taking place but insisted the clear message to Putin was that the war should end.

Albanese, in the Philippines before a meeting of Quad leaders and talks with south-east Asian leaders at the Asean summit, left open the possibility of joining an Apec group photo with Putin if China wished for it to go ahead.

“We think that dialogue is a good thing and we await the outcome of that dialogue,” he said.

“It’s obviously quite significant, the fact that President Trump will be at Asean as well as at Apec, and that we’ll have a Quad leaders meeting as well.

“We want to see something constructive come out of that, including we want to see a de-escalation in the conflicts around the world.”

German’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz , expressed hesitation about the talks at a meeting of EU leaders on Friday.

“I want to state our message to the US very clearly once again: please, no surprises,” he said. “Stay on Team Europe and Team Ukraine , and let us work together for a genuine peace in Ukraine.”

France’s president, Emmanuel Macron , warned against forcing “an unjust peace” on Ukraine and, by extension, all of Europe.

“That is the spirit of defeat,” Macron said. “That is a recipe for another war.”

The meeting has been compared to a 1945 summit at Yalta , in southern Crimea, when then US president, Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin carved up influence across war-ravaged Europe. Zelenskyy has warned that the meeting must not turn into “Yalta 2, 3, 4”.

The historian Timothy Garton Ash has called the trilateral summit, organised after a proposal by Putin last month, “a sort of parody” of Yalta, even as analysts say decisions on the future of Ukraine or China’s ambitions to take control of Taiwan without their involvement is unlikely.

Albanese said the summit would not undercut a growing push by countries including Australia and Canada for middle powers to have greater influence in world affairs.

“We’ll continue to engage with like-minded countries,” he said. “There are two super powers in the world.

“What’s important about the struggle of the people of Ukraine is that they’re not just standing up for their own sovereignty; they’re standing up for the international rule of law.”

Asked if he would join the so-called “family photo” of Apec leaders if Putin took part, Albanese said he would consider the wishes of China as the host nation. But he said the Russian president should know Australia’s opposition to the invasion.

“If he’s in a room where I am, I’m sure they’ll hear my contribution,” Albanese said.

After the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting, Australia’s Penny Wong joined with European and Canadian counterparts to avoid a group photo . It was cancelled by US officials when a third of participants declined to stand alongside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov.

Albanese signed a new defence agreement with the Philippines on Sunday, visiting the supply ship HMAS Stalwart in the Port of Manila. Australia is helping to strengthen the Philippines’ defensive capability against Chinese aggression.

More freedom-of-navigation naval exercises are planned in an attempt to counter Beijing’s efforts to influence the South and East China seas.

stories.title: Workers should get paid time off to train for crises, say peers
stories.summary: A House of Lords committee says more preparation is needed for war, power cuts, and cyber-attacks.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 16 November 2026, 06:04 GMT

Workers should be able to take paid time off to prepare for national emergencies, a House of Lords committee has recommended.

In a report, the peers said a new "civic resilience leave" would enable employees to undertake training and emergency volunteering without losing income.

It is one of a slew of recommendations from a 12-strong committee that has been examining how to make the UK better able to respond to crises including war, power cuts, cyber-attacks and natural disasters.

It comes after the government launched a campaign calling on the British public to stock up on tinned food and bottled water to be prepared for emergencies.

In a report published on Monday, peers on the national resilience committee will say the government's campaign, launched last month, was a "welcome step".

But it will argue that Britain is still underprepared for potential disruption, adding that the public did not have the "full picture" about potential threats from Russia, China and Iran, including cyber attacks.

It will recommend that all local councils should draw up registers of volunteers with "relevant skills and capabilities" to help out during crises, as well as lists of buildings in their area that could be used as emergency shelters.

The government should also launch a national campaign for registered volunteers and civil reservists, it added, modelled on the programme launched by the NHS for "volunteer responders" during the Covid pandemic.

'Proportionate' leave

It noted that the previous government floated the idea of a "civilian reservist cadre" to help out in times of crisis in its 2021 defence review, but this was dropped when the report was updated two years later.

Although some employers offer time off to staff who volunteer, there is currently no legal entitlement to paid leave for those in roles such as coastguard rescue, firefighting, or the St John Ambulance.

Army reservists can claim up to £400 a day , external from the government to cover lost pay if they are mobilised, but employers do not have to allow time off for training - although some choose to do so.

In their report, the peers said a new right to paid time off could cover "approved" training and volunteering, without specifying exact roles.

They did not recommend an exact leave entitlement, instead suggesting that Labour ministers should work with employers to design "proportionate arrangements" for workers.

New preparedness app

Elsewhere in their report, peers recommended the government should send booklets to every household with information about what to do in a crisis, modelled on those sent to homes in Sweden and Denmark.

In its evidence to the inquiry, the government said it planned to provide information through its website - but peers rejected this approach, adding it risked "excluding some groups" and would not work during prolonged periods of disruption.

The peers also recommended the development of a multilingual "public preparedness app" to access official guidance on preparing for emergencies.

It should also allow users to automatically share their location with emergency authorities, similar to the 112 Suomi app in Finland, they added.

The Cabinet Office said it would "carefully review" the report, whilst insisting the government was already taking action to improve crisis resilience.

It pointed to work already under way to update departments' secret defence plans, known as the "war book", and a major exercise scheduled for next year to test the the UK's resilience for war.

The government also recently announced new measures to protect the UK's undersea internet cables, including powers for officials to inspect cable landing stations owned and operated by telecom companies.

stories.summary: The party says its proposals for England aim to address excessive screen time and over-reliance on AI.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 15 November 2026

The Conservatives have promised to halt screen-based exams and cut coursework in a bid to limit the use of AI by schoolchildren in England if the party returns to power.

The party has also pledged to develop new guidelines so that laptops and tablets are not the "default in classrooms".

Shadow education secretary Laura Trott cited recent warnings from clinicians that excessive screen time could be damaging children's health, adding that "everything in schools must be safe for children and improve standards".

The government is currently developing new screen-time guidance for children and has previously said it would consult on the safety of AI in schools.

The vast majority of school exams in the UK are pen and paper based. Under the previous government led by Sir Keir Starmer, exam regulator Ofqual launched a consultation last year , external on the introduction of on-screen exams.

But it emphasised that pen and paper would "remain central" and that the most widely taken subjects would not be moving to digital assessments for the "foreseeable future".

In their announcement on Sunday, the Tories said they would "put a stop" to the introduction of screen-based exams, and require screen time for secondary pupils to be limited to no more than two hours a day.

The party said it would also minimise the amount of coursework in school assessments to avoid lowering educational standards "by allowing children to become overly reliant on the use of generative AI platforms".

Under the plans, primary schools would be required to keep screen use to a minimum and only use screens where necessary, such as in computing lessons.

Phones to be banned from pupils' bags or pockets under stricter rules for schools in England Published 6 days ago

Ministers to issue guidance on children's screen use Published 8 June

The announcement comes after a group of more than 150 clinicians warned last month that the amount of time children in England spend on screens at school could be harming their "physical and developmental health" .

An open letter to Education Secretary Lucy Powell and Health Secretary Yvette Cooper from the clinicians said they were prescribing glasses, hearing aids and speech therapy to children "for a problem that is unintentionally being made worse in our schools".

Trott said: "I want to slash screen use in classrooms and set a new norm where screens are no longer the default. That means no screens in early years, minimal use in primary schools except where required by the curriculum."

Figures from the most recent government survey , external show that in 2024, most teachers (89%) used interactive whiteboards within lessons. But the survey also found that most teachers - 79% in primary and 69% in secondary - said pupils were using individual devices in fewer than a quater of lessons, or not at all.

The Tories said their plans draw on the work of the Health Professionals for Safer Screens campaign group, which has warned about the effects of excessive screen time on children.

Its founder Dr Rebecca Foljambe said: "We have become excessively preoccupied with why children are on screens. Although content is important, this distracts from the fact that daily screen time can profoundly affect a child's health, whatever they are watching or doing."

As part of its proposal, the Tories said £900m that "the government currently spends on EdTech" would be repurposed to create a £250m fund for new textbooks.

A Department for Education spokesperson said schools decided how much to spend on educational technology, which alongside screens also included things such as management information systems, from within their own budgets.

"It is up to schools to decide how they use their funding in the best interests of pupils," they said.

They added: "Building on the guidance we have published for children under 5, in the new year the department will publish clear guidance on screen use for all children aged 5 to 18, giving parents the advice they need."

A ban on smartphones in schools in England came into force in June, making individual schools and trusts legally responsible for being phone-free throughout the day.

Education is a devolved matter in the UK, with each of the four nations managing their own systems.

The UK social media ban for under-16s - banning children from major platforms such as TikTok and Instagram - will come into force in March.
